maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. T. A. Crerar (Minister of Agriculture), the House went into committee on the following proposed resolution; Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend The Meat and Canned Hoods Act, chapter twenty-seven of the Statutes of 1907, and to provide that an establishment a® defined in the said Act shall include any abattoir, packing house or other premises in which any food or food product whiah may be named by the Governor in Council is prepared for food for export or is stored for export; and that all fish, fruit or vegetables, or products thereof, or any food or food products which may be named' by the Governor in Council, used' in any establishment where these articles are prepared for export, shall be sound, wholesome and fit for food; and any such articles or products found in the said establishment unsound or unwholesome shall be confiscated' and destroyed in such manner as may be provided by the regulations ; and also that no person shall offer or accept for export or import, or shall export or import any articles subject to inspection unless the requirements regarding inspection and marking have been complied with in
fSir George Foster.]
respect to such 'articles, and every person offering any carcass, or portion or product thereof, or fruit or vegetable, or products thereof, or food or food products named by the Governor in Council, for export or import, or exporting or importing such carcass, portion or product, or any fruit or vegetable, or products thereof, or food or food products named by the Governor in Council, shall furnish such proof as is required' by the regulations as to whether the articles so offered for export or import, or exported or imported, are subject to inspection or not; and, further, that no carcass or portion of product thereof intended for food shall be imported into Canada unless proof satisfactory to the Minister accompany it that the same has passed Government inspection in the country of origin, and any such carcass or portion or product thereof imported into Canada shall he subject to such further inspection, and shall confirm to such requirements as the-Governor in Council may by regulation prescribe; and that no fruit or vegetables or products thereof, or food or food-products which may be named by the Governor in Council, shall be Imported into Canada or exported from Canada, unless the same conform to such requirements as the Governor in Council may by regulation prescribe; and that any carcass or portion or product thereof, or fruit or vegetable or products thereof, or food or food product, that does not conform to the requirements of sucih regulations shall, upofi condemnation by any inspector, he forfeit to His Majesty, and may be disposed of as the Minister may direct; and, further, that no article subject to inspection shall be offered or sold for export or import, or exported or imported, under any name intended or calculated to deceive as to its true nature; and that no package containing any article subject to inspection shall be marked with any label, brand or mark which falsely represents the quantity or weight or contents of such package; and that n* package containing any article subject to inspection shall be marked with any label, brand or mark which falsely represents the date when the articles or goods contained ^therein were packed.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: I think this is the longest resolution I have ever read, and if the object the minister wishes to attain is simply what he says, he could have attained it by a much shorter resolution. I understand the Minister of Agriculture does not want slaughterhouses doing business in the United States to import into this country meat which is not subject to the same regulation as the meat which is slaughtered in Canada. Is that one of the objects of the resolution?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
Not quite. We want to
put ourselves in the position that we can refuse admission to Canada of products not properly certified to by the inspection system of the country in which they originate.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: From which they issue?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Yes, where they are manufactured.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
I thought the object was to make all such importations into Canada, subject to the same inspection as that to which the product of the Canadian manufacturer is subject to, and I think such a resolution would Ibe more equitable. >If the meat is to conform to the degree of inspection which is required by the country from which it comes, how are we [DOT]going to control it? I understand the minister to say that if meat is imported from the United States, he desires the United States standard to be applied to the meat so imported.
Mr. ORERAR f Yes.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
Why so? Does the minister not think it would be fair to apply to any commodity imported into Canada the same standard as is applied to the Canadian producer? If you are going to have a system of inspection for Canadian produce, why not subject the importation of similar produce to the same standard?
If we are going to consume imported products in Canada let us have one standard that will protect the consumer, and let it be the Canadian standard, instead of the standard of the exporting country.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: We can absolutely control our manufacture in Canada by our own system of inspection. We obviously cannot send our inspectors to the places where these goods are manufactured in the United States. We can examine their regulations as to the purity of the article manufactured in the United States, and if we are satisfied that those regulations sufficiently guard the purity of the goods, then we can admit the article under the certification that it is manufactured under such regulations.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
The resolution seems to go a little further than that. It says:
And also that no person shall offer or accept for export or import.
If a Canadian dealer is going to accept for import those goods coming from the United States, why not subject him to the same inspection as the man Who is producing in Canada? My hon. friend says we are going to examine their regulations, and if we find their regulations protect us sufficiently, why should we require an inspection on this side? My answer is that the regulations may be all right. You are making regulations in this country. Why do you appoint an inspector? Your regulations may be the best in the world, but what would those regulations be worth unless they were complied with? And how will you know they are complied with, unless you have your inspector who will inspect the produce and see that the produce which is offered on the market complies with the requirements enacted by my hon. friend's department for the protection of the consumer? That is what I think was intended by the resolution. Otherwise why should the words, " or offer for import " be necessary? It would only be necessary to say, " shall not be imported," if the theory of the hon. gentleman is to hold good. My objection is to the acceptance of any regulation made by the United States, and the fact that, if you find the regulations satisfactory you 'are going to conclude they have been complied with. It is not the regulation, so much as the compliance with it, that protects the consumer.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Perhaps I am not making myself perfectly clear. As I understand it, it will work out in this way: the inspectors in the United States factories would inspect and supervise the manufacture of these articles.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: American inspectors?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Yes, they would attach the certificate of the American regulations to the manufactured article, and the article could be imported upon such certification. At the present time the American manufacturers can ship into Canada goods that have no certification or inspection whatever.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: I understand that perfectly.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest we should send our inspector to the United States to supervise the manufacture of these goods there?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: No. I say that before such goods are placed on the market, they should be subject to inspection of the Canadian inspector. If I go to the United States and buy twelve cars of beef-

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Or oleomargarine.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: -or oleomargarine-why should I take the certificate of the American inspector? I presume it is all right, but my hon. friend has just stated they were shipping diseased cattle into British Columbia, and one of the reasons why this Act is proposed is to protect the Canadian consumer from the tuberculosis-affected cattle of the adjoining United States territory. If the ordinary Canadian trader thinks Canadians can be fed on tubercular cattle, there might be some United States inspector who would hold the same opinion. I think it would give more confidence if we had the same inspection, and standard and certificate for meat which is imported from the United States as we have for meat produced in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
I might be permitted to say one word on this subject. I think I am within the mark in saying that the proposition of my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) would not be practicable, for the reason that there is an immense trade going on be'tween the United States and Canada, and between various packing establishments in both countries. They would be very seriously interfered with if there were a multiplication of inspection- duties, and for a great many years practically the same system has been adopted in the officially-inspected establishments in the United States and the officially-inspected establishments in Canada. Those regulations being framed according to the very 'best practice, so long as the article coming from the inspection establishments of either Canada or the 
United States bear the stamp of the inspector, showing that they have been inspected, there is free ingress and egress to and from both countries-. But what the Minister of Agriculture is aiming at is to control those imports from- the United States and- have them, subject to the same drastic regulations employed- -by their official inspection in their establishments, and such examples as he gave, for instance, as meat coming into British Columbia affected with tuberculosis, -is quite a vivid illustration that that particular class of product was not subject to the official inspection of the bureau of the United- States. We therefore should have some control of all those unregulated products and exports to our country. But I thinik it would :be a mistake to- demand such a sweeping measure as not to permit or recognize the official inspection of the United States, -because, ii you did that, they would immediately refuse to accept the official stamp of the inspectors of Canada, and you would find a very serious interference with the immense trade of the countries in these products.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: In this matter, I support the views of the Minister of Agriculture and of the -Secretary of State. I infer from the statement of the Minister of Agriculture and the Secretary of State that this will be a reciprocal arrangement with the United States and that they will accept Canadian inspection?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: They do now.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: I understand that undeT the o-ld law we controlled domestic -and export trade, but not import trade. The only difference I can see now is that by this legislation we -are controlling the import trade.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
Before this resolution
carries I think we ought to ask the Minister of Agriculture to let us know one or two things. As I understand the Inspection Act in Canada, the public is the goat. We have been- inspecting -all the stuff we send out of Canada, while a lot of stuff that is consumed in Canada is not inspected at all. For instance, the people of Canada can be -supplied with beef from animals suffering from lumpy jaw and all that sort of thing. Is there any .meat sold by retail in Canada that is subject to inspection?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: For dnterprovincial trade.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
If it is sold for interprovincial trade, it is inspected, but if if is sold locally, it is not inspected. The same applies to a great many other things

that the minister is now taking into consideration. The people of Canada have to take their chance as to the food which is supplied them, but if it goes out of the province, or to a foreign country, it is inspected, and protection is thus afforded to the people of another province or to the foreigner. I think the time has come when the people will demand that there shall be an inspection of all meat that is consumed in Canada, except in the case where a man kills an animal himself and sells the meat by retail. Even in that case some action should be taken. We do not go far enough. We protect the English and the American consumer by a rigid system of inspection, while we allow our own people to be fed with cancerous beef and mutton from abroad and from home.
In reference to t'he cold storage warehouses. Some years ago we had that matter under discussion, and it is a very warm topic at the present time among the people of this country. This idea of permitting cold storage warehouses to keep eggs and chickens and meat in cold storage for eight or ten years and then unload them on the public when the price is high, is something that should receive our immediate attention. The minister should take unto himself the power, as they have in Australia and other countries, to fix a date beyond which it shall not he permitted to keep meats in cold storage. If I get a deer in Muskoka and I put it in cold -storage, I have to take it out of cold storage at the first of the year or I am liable to a fine. Why shouldn't other meats be treated likewise? The way in which the public has been imposed upon by the cold storage warehouses is an outrage. I do not wish to mention any particular name, and it is unnecessary for me to do so in so far as this is concerned, but I do say that the time is ripe for the minister to take action so that regulations may be provided by this Government and this House, which is the moving spirit of the Government, providing that anybody who puts food into cold storage shall be required to take it out before it becomes embalmed.
There are other matters connected with this same problem which, had 1 known this subject was coming up this afternoon, I would have discussed. For instance, there is the resignation of Mr. O'Connor. Everybody in Canada knows that Mr. O'Connor was right on the job in reference to these cold storage warehouses that are referred to in this resolution. Mr. O'Connor tried to do his duty with the result that the public supported him in his administration of the law. He endeavoured to curb these cold storage warehouses, control the profiteers and compel the marketing of products held for storage in them. But, what do we find? We find that Mr. O'Connor, who has been giving such good public service, has been dismissed, or at least takes his own dismissal-JI do not know why or very much about the subject. The public have made up their mind that the interests that control these large warehouses have got this Government and this Parliament by the throat. I think it is time for the members of this House to speak out in no uncertain tone.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: In regard to the import and export of meat, there has long been an understanding between the Bureau of Animal Industry of the United States and our Health of Animals Branch to exchange certificates. The only proper place to make an inspection of meat is on the killing floor, where the offal can be thoroughly inspected at the time the animal is-slaughtered. It would he quite impossible for a man to make a thorough inspection of a dressed carcass. I think it would be asking too much of a Canadian inspector to ask him to inspect the contents of an American sausage. Some of these articles are rather mysteriously made at times. In regard to the inspection of meat, all the meat intended for export or for interprovincial trade, is killed in slaughter houses under inspection,. a brand is placed on the meat passing inspection and you can always he assured of securing good meat if you get meat bearing the Government brand. All the other meat killed in local slaughter houses, if inspected at all, should be inspected by provincial governments or municipalities.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if this resolution covers a case which was presented to me the other night from Toronto. A gentleman there, a dealer who bought eggs largely and retailed them in the city, said that ho had reas'on to believe that eggs were imported from the United States into Canada subject to export. He understood that some privilege had been conceded by the Department of Agriculture permitting of the candling of these eggs in Canada. The result is that Yankee eggs are unloaded on the Canadian market and good Canadian eggs are exported. I w*ould like to know if the Canadian public are now getting candled Yankee eggs and if they are taking.

the place of good Canadian eggs which are sent out for export. Is that possible under the regulations?

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
I do not think the legislation intended to be passed under this resolution covers the point that the hon. member (Sir Sam Hughes) brings up. It is intended to cover the inspection of meats and canned goods under the Meat, and Canned Foods Act.
Sir SAM. HUGHES: It says "foods."

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) who has had a great deal of experience in the administration of this Act, has very exactly, I think, stated the situation. It would be obviously impossible to send our inspectors over to ciosely examine all the material that entered into canned gOods manufactured in the United States. But we can, under the arrangement we have with their Bureau in the United States, admit these goods to Canada under their certificate and be, I think, assured that we are getting only wholesome and proper food. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the other suggestions that are brought up by some hon. members might be discussed in committee on the Bill.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: We are in committee now.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
I would like to make my point clear. The eggs that are imported from the United States are brought into our cold storage warehouses. A gentleman from Toronto told me the other night that the citizens of Canada were being fed on *eggs imported from the southern States subject, under the law, to export. They are brought in under some suspended clause of the Inspection Act permitting these eggs to be examined and candled and if any are found bad they can be replaced by Canadian eggs. .
He had reason to believe, he said, that these eggs were being unloaded on the Canadian market and the Canadian eggs sent on>
for export; in other words, giving the importer the opportunity of bringing in Yankee eggs and sending our Canadian eggs to take their place on the English market. I have heard that the same thing under similar rules has been done with oleomargarine: it has 'been brought in and mixed with the Canadian product and disposed of in this manner. I take this ap-portunity of bringing the facts to the notice of the Minister of Agriculture.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
Has the Minister of Agriculture under consideration the requiring

of Mr. O'Connor's services in regard to the condemnation of any food supplies in packing houses?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Order. I do not think that the hon. gentleman is quite in order in asking who will administer the Act.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
This is a matter in regard to which I think the Minister of Agriculture should go a little further. He undertakes to protect the consumers of Canada in regard to goods that, are imported into this country. That is very well so far as it goes, but I think he should also protect Canadian consumers against the existing method of supplying food products to the people in the large cities of Canada. For example, we have some very large abattoirs in the city of Toronto, as well as branches of Chicago houses, and we have established there a municipal abattoir. Previous to its inception there were many small abattoirs scattered through the city causing a serious nuisance in the residential districts. However, by the establishment of a municipal abattoir, the killing of various kinds of live stock was centralized and made subject to inspection. That policy has helped a great deal, but it is only applicable to Toronto. You may go outside that city and in a good sized town find a small establishment carried on as an abattoir, but not subject to inspection. The same statement applies to the canning of goods. Let me give an illustration of what occurred a few years ago in Toronto, and I think is still occurring today in Chicago. You go to a merchant to purchase canned goods. You may be desirous of having for dinner canned chicken or possibly canned turkey, and you buy what purports to be chicken or turkey, and pay the price demanded for such articles. But what do you get? You get a substitute for turkey or chicken in the shape of immature veal, or calf perhaps only a couple of days old. This kind of canned goods is not subject to inspection, and yet I understand the object of the minister in bringing the present measure forward is to protect Canadian consumers against this shipment into Canada. Why should the Americans, who themselves inspect and reject and prohibit the consumption in that country of immature veal and inferior pork and ibeans be allowed' to send such goods into this country? Inferior canned veal and pork and beans, and goods of that nature will not p;iss inspection in the United States but they are held to be quite good enough for Canada.

The Government cannot be too severe in checking such methods of sending inferior goods into Canada.
At the same time our people should be protected against some of the methods adopted in this country. In my opinion the Minister of Agriculture should go a step further, and provide that- all meats consumed in Canada shall be subject to inspection. The appointment in each village or small community of an inspector may be objected to as expensive; but under a proper regulation that could be done and the expense would not be material.	It is
simple enough to provide that in a certain township the killing of hogs, sheep, cattle, calves, and other live-stock shall be subject to inspection. The people of the township, knowing that inspection was obligatory, some central point could be fixed where the killing might be done and one inspector could devote three days to inspection work in that township.	By a
proper apportionment of the time it would be possible for the same inspector to cover several townships, and in that way the expense would not be very great. By such a method you could prevent improper and unhealthy meat from reaching the consumer.
In the case of live stock coming to the Toronto stockyards, an unscrupulous drover who was aware of the strict inspection in force would realize at once that he could not market his animals on the stockyards, and therefore he would immediately ship them to some outside section, where they could be slaughtered and the flesh prepared and afterwards consigned to the Toronto market, and thus escape inspection. Again, in the case of the individual farmdr, 'he might kill seven or eight hogs, a couple of head of cattle, and half a dozen sheep and dispose of the meat on the Toronto market without undergoing inspection, a thing which could not be done in the case of animals slaughtered at the stockyards. The fact that there 'has Jbeen no inspection reduces the market value of the meat, but a speculator might obtain full value for goods that merited condemnation. Therefore, I say the Minister of Agriculture should go far enou'gh to protect the Toronto consumers that are consuming Canadian goods which have not passed inspection, and that can be done at very little expense.
So far as goods that are being imported into Canada are concerned, the minister cannot be too strict in enforcing inspection. If that were done the consuming public would be satisfied. Not only should there be such a system of inspection, but I think
that all canned goods-, whether meats, fruits, or products of other kinds, should have the date stamped upon the can. The longer such goods are kept the less value they possess, and the consumer purchasing canned goods bearing the stamp of the manufacturers would be able to see from the date whether the goods were one year old or entering upon the second year. Such goods depreciate every three or four months, until after a short time they become of no value, but if the date of manufacture is legibly placed on the can the consumer can see just what he is getting.
I repeat, that in my opinion the minister is going in the right direction, only he is not going quite far enough. When the Bill goes to committee I have no doubt we shall have some further suggestions from him, and, perhaps, amendments will be forthcoming which will meet the approval of the House and the community at large.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Thomas Foster) is entirely wrong in hie statements with respect to the inspection of canned goods. I want to tell him that we have inspectors for canned vegetables, fruit, and also poultry, and have had them for yeafe. I am connected with a company that has been in business, more or less, for thirty years. We did not have our products inspected during the greater portion of that period, but for the last six or seven years there have been inspectors. These inspectors remain all the time in the factory until the Government stamp is put on the cans, and under this system the public is adequately protected.
The hon. gentleman has spoken of the necessity of stamping canned goods. I want to tell him that if canned- goods are properly packed and kept in -a proper place the quality will be as good years afterwards as it is at the time the goods -are put up. With respect to fruits and vegetables we do not want to put the dates on the cans, because any one going into a store, if they see goods two years old, would not want to buy them, even though they are just as good as the day they were packed. We have in our factories, for instance, corn which we have kept for twenty years on purpose to see how long it can be pre-. served. The only difference you can see in corn kept that long is in the colour. But, as I said, Mr. Chairman, if you want to destroy the canned goods business, simply put the dates on the labels, because the consumer in buying canned goods will naturally look for the goods packed that year. Canned goods are as good five or six years

after packing as the day they were packed. I know this, because I have been canning for a long time, and we have made the test for our own satisfaction. I would be very sorry to have the minister put the date on the labels of canned goods for the reasons I have mentioned.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to see that the Minister of Agriculture is taking steps to have a more thorough inspection of meats, food and food products. An hon. gentleman stated a few moments ago that some of these goods were mysteriously prepared, and I sincerely believe that he is right. I shall endeavour, if I may be permitted, to give a brief explanation of this matter. But before doing so, I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention to have qualified veterinary surgeons act as inspectors of live stock, or if anyone else may be appointed to such positions? I may say that while I was in the legislature of the state of Montana, in 1901, I was the father of a similar Bill providing for the appointment of inspectors of meats and food, and the Bill provided that up to the time that the cattle went on the killing floor the inspection was to be made by a veterinary surgeon, and no one else. For the inspection of mbats in the refrigerators, or in the markets, it provided that a man well versed in meats was to be appointed, one knowing all the stages from the time the animal is killed until the meat is sold to the consumer.
Now, coming to the preparation of ham, one of the reasons why that should be well inspected is simply because the packers are taking advantage of all the opportunities which are given them, and even -if the opportunity is not. given to them they take it. Take, for instance, to begin with, the brine, which is composed, of course, of water, salt, brown sugar and preservaline; and we all know that preservaline contains acid. Preservaline is put in in order to preserve the meat a longer time. When it comes to the smoking process, instead of smoking it twenty, thirty or forty days, the length of time required to smoke a good ham, it is simply put in a receptacle of some kind with colorine in it. This colorine contains acid also. These things are not very good for the stomach, still the consumer has to take the product. Now, the reason why these things are done is because the ham requires but very little smoking if it is coloured, and it has a very transparent colour, a very nice colour indeed. If it was smoked thoroughly, the ham would drip, that is, the brine in it would drip off. and it would lose weight.

Hence the necessity for the packer not to smoke it in order to retain the weight. The same process is used in regard to breakfast bacon. I may say a word or two about sausages.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Oh, don't.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: That is the article which is the most mysteriously prepared, I believe.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: As a rule, to begin with, they take from fifteen to twenty per cent of pork fat, and then from twenty-five to thirty per cent of beef scraps, or bits of whatever they can find, trimmings as we probably term it; and then about twenty per cent of Victoria or potato flour; and the balance is water. You have about thirty per cent of water in your sausages, and twenty per cent of potato or Victoria flour. When a consumer gets sausage, he pays for the potato flour, the water, the scraps of beef, etc. But when he comes to put the sausage in the frying pan it almost walks out; it won't stay there until the water is all out of it. For these, reasons, and there are a great many others that have been given by other hon. gentlemen, I believe that we ought to have a very thorough inspection of meats at all times, and I hope that the Minister of Agriculture will do his best and finish the good work that he has started along this line.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
I do not see very much objection to the adoption of the resolution. I am heartily in accord with the minister in his endeavour to do everything possible to ensure that the people have better service from our cold storage systems and also from the abattoirs of the country. I merely wish to add that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pelletier), in naming over the different methods of curing bacon, hams and sausages, forgot to mention the one well known during the past election, as post-curing. That is one method which it might be well to have drawn to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, so that when this resolution is passed, and when legislation is introduced along this line, any person, whether in high standing in this country, or an officer of the Government, whether connected with abattoirs, cold storage, or other great institutions, will be prohibited from using a method of that kind. When legislation is passed providing for the appointment of inspectors, only men who are capable and fearless probably will be considered by the minister. He should not

overlook the fact that Mr. O'Connor who occupied the position of cost of living commissioner in this country has the respect of the people of Canada, and not only their respect, but their confidence. Mr. O'Connor fearlessly carried on the duties of his office. Yet we now find that he is allowed to he relieved of office, while the man who is chairman of the Imperial Munitions Board, and an officer of the Canadian Government, still holds office. I do not believe that there is a man on either side of this House, Independent, Liberal or Unionist, who could have stood upon the public platforms throughout Canada in the last election and said that he would support the dismissal of Mr. O'Connor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: Order. I ruled a few moments ago that the dismissal of Mr. O'Connor should not be introduced into this debate. My hon. friend is going altogether too far.

speechtext: I am quite willing to abide 'by your Tuling, Mr. Chairman, but I did not tion. The remarks of the member for North Simcoe was referring to the matter. maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: I have not sufficient information to enable me to discuss the practice or procedure in regard to meat and meat products, but I have information regarding the treatment of vegetables and fruits which, I think, may be of some advantage to the minister in dealing -With this question of provision for inspection. It had previously been the practice to inspect prepared vegetables, pre-4 p.m. pared soups, and the like, at the time of shipment at the seaboard-Halifax, Montreal, St. John, as the case might be. As a result, manufacturers incurred very 'heavy expense and were liable to loss, because if the product was condemned it bad to be shipped back and disposed of to the best advantage. That was brought to the attention of the minister, and I was responsible in some measure for . the change that was made. Afterwards the department appointed inspectors resident at the different manufacturing points, who were supposed to see that the products turned out by these manufactories were at least fit for human consumption. My attention has been particularly called to some cases tbait occurred since the war broke out. The Government entered into large contracts for the supplying of vegetables to the armies overseas-and I speak particularly of vegetable soups, which have been shipped overseas in veTy large quantities. Under the system of inspection that now prevails, these'produots are inspected at the factory and go to the front without any .further examination, and with no possible chance of loss to the producer. But I heard a returned soldier upon the public platform say quite recently, in the .presence of the manufacturer, that although the soldiers went oveT to Europe to kill the Huns, when they ate that soup they felt more like killing the -manufacturer than like killing the Hun-s. Evidence was forthcoming to show that -in the manufacture of these goods, which bad passed the inspection 0-f the officer appointed by the department, celery had been used which had been lying in the warehouse from the days of the South African war. It was ground and prepared, but not shipped, and it had become the habitation of rafts, mice, cobwebs, flies, and all sorts of other unnecessary ingredients. This was used in the manufacture of soup supplied to our .soldier boys at the front. Testimony to this effect was made by men who were actually employed by the manufacturer; yet the inspector appointed by the department had failed to discover that, or had overlooked it.

Before the minister brings in his Bill I would suggest that he provide against meats being kept in cold storage warehouses beyond a certain period. I trust the minister will provide in the Bill for giving the people of this country control over these cold storage warehouses, which I understand are the main factor in the tremendous increase in food prices. If the cold storage warehouses were compelled to market the goods they have in storage at stated periods, after being put in, instead of being allowed to carry them for two or three years, the people would get food a great deal cheaper. It is an injustice "to the public to permit such a monopoly as this to spring up. If the minister would look at the Acts that have been pased in the province of Victoria, Australia, I think he would find something to help him in framing an Act that would be of some benefit to the public. Canned goods, if properly canned, will last for ten years, but if not properly canned, they will not last ten days; that is the whole sum and substance -of the trouble. But this is to be borne in mind. A great quantity of the canned goods coming into this country are imported from other countries than the United States. A vast quantity of beef, for instance, have been imported from the Argentine Republic, and no doubt it is

still finding its way into this country. Eggs from iChina are also co-ming in, some of them twenty years old, no doubt. The minister should take these things into consideration and should be empowered to provide regulations from time to time to cover cases as they arise, such as the bad chicken that had to be cremated in Winnipeg. The minister in Australia has power to frame regulations and stop these abuses.
I know the Minister of Agriculture is desirous of doing everything he can to protect the public and we must all give him credit for his sincerity in that regard. I am sure he will be fearless in doing his duty.
iMr. CLEMENTS:	Is it intended that
every manufacturer of canned goods shall have his monogram or the firm's name on every can of his product? I have heard a good deal said about cold storage warehouses this afternoon, and, am bound to say that if some of the gentlemen who have referred to cold-storage abuses had gone into the subject a little more fully, they would have realized the benefits of cold storage better than they do. The reason I ask the question is this-on the Pacific coast, and on the Atlantic coast too, there is a very great difference in the grades of fish caught at different places along the coast. A certain fish, whether it he a chum salmon, a dog salmon or a cohoe salmon, is of very much better quality in one section of the province of British Columbia than in another, and it would be very unfair for a manufacturer putting up chum or dog salmon along one section of the Pacific coast of British Columbia to have his pack compared with, say, a northern or a southern pack. I have always contended that the manufacturer should place his name or his firm's name on every can, whether it be in the province of British Columbia or in any other province, and I sincerely hope that the minister will see that every manufacturer of canned goods in Canada stands behind his own brand and has his name printed on every can in [DOT]his product.

I should like to refer for a moment to the suggestion made by the horn, member for Toronto (Mr. Thomas Foster), that this Bill does not go far enough. As I understand it, this Bill deals only with the inspection of foods intended for import or export, and it has perhaps escaped the attention of the Government that a great proportion of the meats consumed by the people of this country are not imported. In not only the smaller cities but the larger
cities as well a good proportion of the meat is slaughtered by the farmers in the country and is brought into the city markets and there disposed of to the consumer
Of that food, I think, there is absolutely no inspection and no guarantee that it is fit for human consumption. I am quite ready to admit that in most cases there can be no fault found with the kind of beef and pork that is brought into the markets of the cities. In the city of Kitchener, from which I come, the suggestion has been made at times that all foods brought into the city for sale should have some kind of inspection. We considered that matter for years, and were not able to find a solution, largely because the matter of inspection led to too great an expense, and placed a heavy burden either upon the farmer who produced the food, or else upon the consumer, and under present conditions, where foods are very expensive, and especially meats, perr haps it is not the time to deal with the matter. I would like to make the suggestion that if the Government could direct its attention to that phase of the matter, so that all meat which ordinarily would require in-specion should be inspected with possibly the assistance of the Department of Agriculture, I think a great service would be rendered to the consumers of the cities and towns. Perhaps this is not the place to make that suggestion, but I do so because the hon. gentleman from Toronto (Mr. Thomas Foster) mentioned it, and because I believe it is very well worth considering.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
I might say, with respect to the observation of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and of some other hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the subject that the scope of the Meat and Canned Foods Act is to cover the inspection of articles for interprovincial trade or for export. No matter how desirable it may be to extend the scope and operation of the Act to cover all goods offered for sale, there are obvious difficulties in the way. For instance, a man manufactures sausage, bacon or ham, and brings it into his local market to sell. Very practical difficulties are presented in the creation of a Dominion system of inspection that will adequately inspect, and I believe such inspection for consumption within the province where '.t originates is under provincial regulation, and quite within provincial and municipal power, and the purpose has been to secure a safeguard in that respect through municipal and provincial regulation, leaving to the Dominion the

matter of controlling inspection where the article is'for provincial trade or for export.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext: I should like to get an answer to the question asked by the hon. member for iMatane (Mr. Pelletier). I listened with astonishment to the statement made by the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter). Goods were manufactured in Canada for export and were shipped across the ocean, to be consumed by Canadian soldiers. It is very painful to have to hear such statements as that made by the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. Porter). Can we not get from the Minister of Agriculture a statement of what he intends to put in his Bill? I think it would be proper he should define the qualifications of the inspectors, if he is going to have any. The Bill is generally prepared at the same time as the resolution. The discussion on this resolution is to enlighten the 'House, or to suggest to my hon. friend certain things which occur to the minds of hon. members of this House, according to the knowledge they are able to impart. Why not tell us what will be the qualifications or requirements necessary under this Act for the man to be appointed inspector in order that the people of Canada may expect good service, and have good men in this most important position? Because, after all, the health and welfare of the community depends a good deal upon these people, their honesty and technical knowledge. The hon. gentleman from Matane (Mr. Pelletier) asked, in the case of slaughter houses, if licensed veterinary surgeons would not be appointed. Why not put it in the Bill that, for certain classes of inspection, only men of certain qualifications shall be appointed? This would, at the same time relieve the minister from the burden of patronage. In spite of all the confidence I have in the Civil Service Act, which will he discussed in a few days, I am afraid there will be some loopholes yet, where some fellows will have enough brass, in spite of the law, to walk up to the Minister of Agriculture and say, " I want to be appointed inspector of this or that," and if the applicant does not come within the four corners of the statute, my hon friend will only say, " I cannot appoint you, there is the Law." It will help him, and will give a great deal of satisfaction to the consumers of this country.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
The regulations at present in effect governing the control and inspection of Canadian products provide for the very point my hon. friend raises. Every 
abattoir or packing-house established in Canada is required to have qualified veterinarians to supervise the work. 'They are assisted by lay inspectors who need not be qualified veterinarians, but whose qualifications must be such as to satisfy the Dominion Director General of Veterinary Service that they are fit for the position. It is not expected or contemplated under this that additional inspectors will be Created. There will not be any need for it so far as I can see. The admission of products from other countries oan be supervised by the customs officers who will see that the proper certificates are attached to the article before it is admitted. I appreciate just as fully as my hon. friend the importance of having these goods thoroughly and properly inspected. I assure him that, as far as the possibility of patronage entering into the administration of this Act is concerned, I have no hesitation in making the declaration that it is absolutely not going to enter into it, as far as my administration is concerned. We .have suffered considerably in Canada from the injection of the patronage evil into Government service, and it is time in my judgment that it was eliminated from it.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
So far the Minister of Agriculture -and all t'he other members of the Cabinet have dodged the issue raised by the hon. member for West Hastings. I think the condition of things exposed to the Canadian people to-day deserves a statement from the Government. If such conditions of inspection exist in one factory, as stated by the hon. member for Hastings, I would be ready to believe the same condition existed in other factories throughout the country. Had the question been raised on this side of the House, t'he Government might have thought it was a political attack, but it has been raised on the other side of the House, and I think we are entitled to a statement on this question.
Mr. 'CRERAR: I would say, in reply to the hon. member for Hastings, that, of course,
I have no knowledge of the case cited by him. I have no hesitation Whatever in saying that such condition of affairs should not be permitted to exist. I take it that this happened some time ago, and I shall certainly take the opportunity to investigate the matter and obtain all the information I can upon it.

maintopic: MEAT AND CANNED FOODS ACT AMEND MENT.
speechtext:
This subject is undoubtedly a very technical one, and I believe, after a discussion of an hour and a half, we do not yet understand fully the

extent or purport of the resolution. The hon. gentleman from West Hastings has brought before the House a case in which the law was violated. Of course, it may have been the result of an accident, but as to what the facts are we are not very clear. But the fact to which I want to draw the attention of the Minister of Agriculture is that this cannot have the effect of improving the law as it is now but rather of emasculating it. If I understand this resolution aright, it will not make the law more rigid but it will reduce the rigidity of the law and make possible its evasion. The law we have to-day, the Act passed in 1907 provides that all food, whether animal or vegetable, shall pass inspection. There is no exception to it. Here is the letter of the law, section 3:
All animals intended for slaughter in any establishment shall be inspected as provided by the regulations.
No animal shall be allowed to enter the parts of an establishment where slaughtering is carried on, unless it has undergone such inspection and been found to be healthy and fit for food.	'
Section 13 of the Act reads:
AH fish, fruit or vegetables used in any establishment where these articles are prepared for export, shall be sound, wholesome, and fit for food ; and any such articles or products thereof found in the said establishment unsound or unwholesome shall be confiscated and destroyed as provided by the regulations.
Under these two sections all animals, fish, fruit and vegetable foods must go into an establishment. By the Act the word "establishment" is defined and what is the definition?
"Establishment" means any abattoir, packing house, or other premises in which such animals are slaughtered, or in which any parts thereof or products thereof, or fish, or fruit, or vegetables. are prepared for food or export or are stored for export.
Again we find the definition of the word "food":
"Food" includes every article used for food or drink by man, and every ingredient intended for mixing with the food or drink of man for any purpose.
This means that all kinds of food, without any exception, which are to be exported, shall have to pass through this examination. No exception is made. What, however, is the principle of my resolution of my hon. friend? Instead of having this rigid provision that all food must be inspected, that there may be no exception, the law is to be emasculated by substituting the will of the Governor in Council for the rigidity of the law and the will of Parliament. Here is the resolution and I call the attention of my hon. friend to it.
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend The Meat and Canned Foods Act, chapter twenty-seven of the statutes of 1907, and to provide that an establishment as defined in the said Actwhich I have just read-
-shall include any abattoir, packing house or other premises in which any food or food product which may be named by the Governor in Council is prepared for food for export or is stored for export.
This means that instead of, as we have to-day, the rigid letter of the law that all food for man must be inspected and must pass through this establishment, the Governor in Council has it in his power to say, in his wisdom, that any kind of food shall, or shall not, be inspected. It may be poultry. it may he bacon, it may be .anything else; the Governor in Council has the power to except from the provisions of the law any food that he thinks it proper to except. That is not making the law more rigid than it was before. It is giving to the Government a dangerous power because it seems to me that there should be no exception at all and that all food should be inspected. The Governor in Council should not have the power to except any food from that inspection. In that respect the resolution is certainly emasculating the Act as it is at present and I call the attention of the Minister of Agriculture to it. For my part, I have no doubt of his good intentions; I give him every credit for them, I do not think he has been the draughtsman of this resolution, I think he should take into his very serious consideration the question as to whether he should ask Parliament to adopt such a provision as that.

I can assure the committee that it was not the intention to have the construction put upon this resolution which the right hon. the leader of the Opposition attaches to it. It is possible that the resolution may be faultily draughted, but I shall read the amendment which it is proposed to make to'Section B of the Act, defining the meaning of "establishment. (B) "establishment" means any abattoir, packing house, or other premises in which such animals are slaughtered, or in which any parts thereof or products thereof, or fish, or fruit, or vegetables, are prepared for food for export or are stored for export.
With the addition that ic proposed to 'be made, it will read as follows:
(B) "establishment" means any abattoir, packing house, or other premises in which such animals are slaughtered, or in which any pants thereof or products thereof, or fish, or fruit or vegetables or any food or food products

which may be named by the Governor in Council, are prepared for food for export or are stored for export.
If I understand the argument of my right hon. 'friend, it is that the addition of the words "or any food or food products which maybe named by the Governor in Council" limits the preceding words?

The idea we had in mind was to cover all additions to these present categories of food; that is to say, some food that might be manufactured or invented and which would not be covered by the preceding words. Take, for instance, condensed milk. Condensed milk would not be included unuer the definition as it previously stood. At any rate, that was the purpose of the addition to the definition of the term "establishment." I shall be very glad to take the suggestion of my right hon. friend, which, I admit, is a very important one, into consideration and discuss it with the officials of the department.
Sir WILFRID LAU'RIER:	I would be
very glad if my hon. friend would do that. But, let me call his attention to the fact that condensed milk is an article of food. Let me again refer my hon. friend to the definition of " food":
"Pood" includes every article used for food or drink by man, and every ingredient intended for mixing with the food or drink of man for any purpose.
_ This includes condensed milk. The objection I have to this provision is that the Governor in Council takes it into his power to remove from the disposition of this Act any kind of food whatever. The law should be left as it is that all food should be subject to inspection.

What is the necessity

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.
ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Crerar (Minister of Agriculture) the House went into committee on the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, chapter seventy-five of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, as amended by chapter six of the statutes of 1913, and to provide that the Governor in Council may order a compensation to be paid .to the owners of animals slaughtered under the provisions of the Act, the value of the animal to be determined by the Minister or by some person appointed by Mm, but the value, except as otherwise provided by the Aot, not

to exceed In the case of grade animals two hundred dollars for each horse, eighty dollars for each head of cattle and twenty dollars for each pig or sheep, and in the case of pure bred animals five hundred dollars for each horse, two hundred and fifty dollars for each head of cattle and seventy-five dollars for each pig or sheep. These amendments to remain in operation for three years.
Mr. 'CRERAR: I think a word of explanation will suffice 'for this resolution. At the time this Act was originally passed the values upon which compensation was based for the slaughter of condemned animals were fixed by statute, in the case of cattle $60 per head and for pigs and sheep $15 per head, and the compensation allowed when animals were condemned and slaughtered was two-thirds of the value set by statute. Owing to the increased value of these animals at the present time, the compensation allowed when they are ordered to be destroyed does not adequately compensate their owners. The intention of the Act when originally drafted, as I understand it, was to encourage the reporting to the proper authorities of animals which might be affected by some contagious disease, so that they could be properly examined, and, if found a menace, destroyed. I think it is only proper that now, when the value of these animals has increased, and in some cases doubled, beyond what it was at the time the Act was originally passed, that the limit upon which compensation can toe fixed should be raised, and that is the purpose of the resolution.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.

Mr. WM. SMITH: I would like to congratulate the minister upon having taken a step in the right direction. The owner of live animals found to be suffering from contagious disease may not be at fault and therefore he should be recouped in some way or other. I do not find fault with the minister's figures so far as thoroughbred animals .are concerned, but I do not think he has gone far enough in connection with the grades. The compensation fixed for grade horses is all right. But it does not take much of an animal, in the case of cattle, to be worth $80. The minister should have gone at least $120. In the case of swine, we all know that, at 20 cents a pound it does not take much of a hog to represent $20. I would suggest that that amount be raised to $30, leaving the compensation, for sheep as it is. I would suggest to the minister that, when he introduces his Bill, it should .be on the lines indicated here today.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I .agree with the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Smith) that there might be a slight advance made in regard to grade cattle. I feel satisfied that the minister is taking a step in the right direction, but I question if he is going quite far enough. The great difficulty we have had .in Ontario in regard to swine and cattle which is condemned a.t different abattoirs, is that a percentage is deducted from the buyers, and the buyers deduct it from the producers. That has caused a great deal of dissatisfaction. The Government have inspectors in the abattoirs where the stock is slaughtered, and when a diseased animal is condemned, the cost comes back either on tihe buyer or on the seller to the extent of one-half of one per cent, which is deducted by the buyer from all the purchases that he makes throughout the country. Some buyers deduct from the seller; some stand the loss themselves. But the



abattoirs exact that percentage from all the buyers irrespective of whether it comes out of the farmer or not. I believe the time is opportune for the minister to extend his legislation a little farther, and since the condemning is done by his own officers, instead of a deduction being made from an innocent party it would be well if the< Government were to make an allowance to overcome that, and so do away with the inconvenience, annoyance and dissatisfaction which occurs from time to time. I believe that last year, or the year before last, the packing houses, when extracting one-half ,of one per cent for this purpose alone, made a net profit of $165,000 above the value of what was really condemned, judging from figures which I have secured from the Department of Agriculture. This is a matter which I would be very glad to have the minister give his serious thought and attention to, and if he can effect a reform, it would be heartily appreciated and accepted with good-will by all the producers throughout Canada.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In introducing this resolution, the minister stated that he did so on account of the increase in value of animals in recent years. That statement is right enough, but it seems to me that the result of his arithmetic has been defective, because, as stated by the hon. member for South Ontario, the compensation allowed for a horse is altogether out of proportion to that given for a good dairy animal, that is, in proportion to their earning value today. The value of a horse has not increased since the previous regulations were put in force; it has rather decreased. But the value of dairy cattle has increased enormously, and it seems to me that the minister might readjust that and give a fair compensation for dairy animals.
There is another feature of this matter which is deserving of consideration by the minister while he is dealing with this subject, and that is the prevention of tuberculosis. I am told by stockmen that there are many ways in which tuberculosis is spread throughout this country. One way in particular, which is a grievance of the stockmen, is in the importation of cattle from the Old Country. Take, for instance, cattle shipped from the Old Country to the United States via Canada. These cattle arrive at the quarantine station at Levis, and they are there tested, and if there are reactors in a herd they are not allowed to enter the United States, and they are not shipped back to the Old Country, but they are earmarked and allowed to go about 
through the herds in Canada spreading disease among Canadian animals. I think the minister should give that matter his serious consideration, and stop that practice.
There is another matter which has been pointed out by stock men which might prevent somewhat the spread of tuberculosis in dairy animals, and that is that any man calling an auction sale-when a man buys at a private sale he is running certain chances, but that is his own business- should he compelled to give a certificate that the herd is free of disease. I submit these suggestions for the consideration of the minister.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, being fairly well versed in the value of dairy cattle, I am of opinion that the compensation of $80 placed on these animals is altogether too little. It is a well known fact that the price of dairy cattle this last year has risen from twenty-five to forty per cent. We cannot get any kind of dairy cattle at the present time for less than $140 or $150, and even up to $180. I think that the man who has the misfortune to have dise.ase enter his herd should not be paid off with $80, when lit has cost him double or treble that amount for his animal. I think the minister might go a little further, and put the amount at $100 or $120; which would, to a certain extent, meet the lass sustained. So far as the compensation for horses is concerned, I have no fault to find with that, but in the case of other animals, especially swine, the compensation is hardly enough. The compensation to be paid for dairy cattle is a very important consideration, especially in eastern Ontario, alt the present time. I have no doubt but that., when the minister thinks the matter over, and takes into consideration the prices we have to pay, he will naaise the amount of compensation for dairy cattle.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would like to bring a matter to the attention of the Minister of Agriculture, when drafting the Bill which is to be presented to the House, in order to obviate an 'injustice which I think was done to a resident in my constituency. I was not a member of this House when this was brought to my notice, and I have not all the details in my memory now, hut I remember that this farmer told me the circumstances, which entailed a heavy loss, in the neighbourhood of $2,000, compensation for which was refused by the Department of Agriculture. This man had a large herd of hogs, and a representative of the Government claimed that his hogs weTe

infected wiith cholera. Against the protestations of the owner, the hogs were slaughtered. The inspector first slaughtered a couple, but did not find any indications of cholera, as the farmer informed me. I understand that when a hog has cholera the disease is shown in the lung. Although he did not find any traces of cholera, he insisted on slaughtering the entire hundred hogs. Afterwards, he stated that he would make a report to the Government, and that the man would he paid for his hogs. At the time this man was speaking to me, he had not heard what had become of that inspector, nor had he been paid for his hogs-and this was eight months ago. Apparently the inspector, seeing he had made a mistake, made himself scarce, and I do not know whether even the department knows where the man is. Would it not be well, in drafting this legislation, to provide that when a veterinary or inspector condemns a man's stock he should, before destroying it, give the owner a certificate so that the owner will have something to show that his stock has been condemned and slaughtered? There should be some way of providing against such an injustice as that to which I have referred.

maintopic: ANIMAL CONTAGIOUS DISEASES ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to state that I approve entirely the principle of this resolution, but that I cannot accept the opinion of the hon. Minister of Agriculture as regards one of its provisions. I find that the fee, under the terms of that legislation, in the case of dairy cattle slaughtered, is not sufficient, the resolution provides that in the case of grade animals, two hundred dollars will be allowed for every horse and eighty dollars for every head of cattle. I am satisfied that this amount is inadequate especially at the present time. The price for dairy cattle has considerably increased of recent date and such increase will be more in evidence in the near future; the reason is that the supply is much more restricted for that kind of stock than it is for horses, for instance. As a matter of fact, it is much more difficult to get good dairy cattle than any other kind of farm animals. .Considering the enhanced prices for dairy, I am of opinion that a higher rate of compensation for dairy cattle should be fixed and I trust the Minister of Agriculture will duly consider this suggestion.
