maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.

speechtext:
Right Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved second reading bf Bill .No. 32, respecting the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
He said: At the time of the adoption of the resolution upon which this Bill is founded, I said I would make some explanation of the Bill on its second reading.
I shall do so as briefly as I possibly can. The Bill does not institute a new department; the amendments are designed to improve and broaden the Act and ensure its better working. Perhaps I might outline briefly the development of 5 p.m. our statistical work in Canada from the time of Confederation -without, of course, going into history. Our statistics fat first centred upon the taking of the decennial census. The first census was taken in 1870. Legislation was ' enacted for the taking Of that census, but no permanent census or statistics office was established. Again in 1879 there was legislation for the taking of the decennial census, and three censuses were taken on that legislation. In 1905 there was a complete revision of the Census and Statistics Act. The office was made permanent; the staff was made permanent and the scope was broadened so as to include general statistics. The work went on with a gradual accretion and extension in the different departments, and in 1912 the branch was transferred to the Department of Trade and Commerce. No uniform and co-ordinated system of statistics had been established, and the method was not at all in keeping with the necessities of the case.
A departmental commission was appointed in 1912, composed of Richard Grigg, Commissioner of Commerce at that time, Chairman; Professor Adam Shortt, Civil Service Commissioner; Ernest Henry Godfrey, Census and Statistics Branch ; W. A. Warne, Statistical Branch of the Department of Trade and Commerce; Robert Hamilton Coats, Department of Labour, and John R. K. Bristol, Department of Customs. This commission instituted a thorough examination of the system, as it affected both Dominion and provincial work and summarized their conclusions. I do not think I could do better than read an extract from the report of that commis-

sion, which briefly states the general situation.
Though many of the statistical reports issued by various departments are of undoubted excellence, there is apparent in the body of Canadian statistics, considered' as a whole, a lack of coherence and common purpose. This is traceable to imperfect appreciation in the past of the fact that the statistics of the country should constitute a single harmonious system, with all divisions in due oo-relation. Under the British North America Act, 1867, the Dominion is given specific authority to deal with "statistics," and while this must not be regarded as precluding statistical activity on the part of local governments, it does apparently imply that statistics are a matter of national concern and may therefore properly come under the general coordinating authority of the Federal Government. No such viewpoint or function, however, has in the past been assumed. The effect statistically has been to inculcate routine and the neglect of opportunities for furnishing wider information and service. "While this detachment has characterized the departments of the Dominion Government, still more has it been evident as between the several provinces and the Dominion, and between province and province, notwithstanding that the national importance of many of the functions of the provincial governments under confederation calls urgently for statistical uniformity and homogeneity. This general condition we would consider to be the fundamental defect which must be met and overcome in the existing situation. Some of the unfortunate results which have followed may be briefly Indicated:	'
1.	The scope of Canadian statistics has been restricted. On not a few points of vital interest to the country little or no statistical information exists. There has been no general answer to the question, what statistics should a country such as Canada possess? What are the phenomena requiring the scientific measurements supplied by statistics if Canadian national development is to proceed to the best advantage?
2.	Where the statistical activities of several bodies working along similar lines are virtually independent, duplication is inevitable.
3.	The statistics are unequal in quality and value. The absence of leadership is nowhere more apparent than in the varying extent to which statistical methods have been developed in the different branches.
4.	The restriction of outlook has impaired promptitude in the issue of reports.
6. Lack of unity and co-ordination prevents true comparisons between Canada and other countries. The recent growth of international intercourse has rendered such comparisons more than ever necessary, and they have become indispensable to the national progress of Canada.
That, in short, is a eharaoteiization of the impression which was left on the commission after its examination was completed. A remedy was suggested by the commission, and I will take the liberty of reading a short extract to give the essentials of their recommendation. They suggested:
1. That there be created a Central Statistical Office to organize in co-operation with the

several departments concerned, the strictly statistical work undertaken by the Dominion Government. The Object of this organization should toe to co-ordinate the statistics of Canada under a single comprehensive scheme and so to extend them that they may meet the present needs of the country and follow the probable course of its development. To borrow a phrase employed in a similar connection by an eminent statistician, the object of such a reorganization should be primarily to constitute a "central thinking office" on the subject of the statistics of Canada. Describing the possible functions of such an office Mr. Bowley wrote:	"Such
an office must have cognizance of all the statistics of more than departmental Importance which are published officially. Misleading statistics must he suppressed, overlapping must be stopped, Careful plans must he devised1 for filling in the gaps at present left, and preparations made for investigation of matters likely to become of public importance. All hills involving or affecting the collection of statistics should be considered by it. Publications for the use of the public should in some cases he edited by it, with careful definitions and with short analyses and criticisms, stating accurately and intelligently the purport and meaning of their contents. In other cases, where a department already exists for such publications, there should be coordination with a view to carrying out the purposes already indicated."
This so well expresses our own views as to the scope and functions which the proposed Canadian office should assume that we cannot do better than allow it to stand as a part of our report, adding that the examples of Germany and Austria show that the idea is (both practicable and valuable.
2. In order to give effect to this recommendation it may be necessary to enact further legislation or to amend the present Census and Statistics Act.
The House has now before it the condition of things as it appeared to the commission, and their recommendations as to what should be done to remedy that condition. Since that time different steps have been taken in respect of modelling and preparation for broader work, and1 for more coordination between the branches gathering statistics. What was found and hinted at by the commission was this:	A system of
gathering general statistics over and above the departmental or adininistrative statistics had gradually grown up in some departments, and in consequence there was overlapping and lack of uniformity in method, and that took away from the authority of the general conclusions arrived at. What was also taking place was that outside of Dominion statistics the different provinces were gradually branching out into statistical work necessitated, in the first place, by their administrative wants. Different branches under provincial administration, say Mines or Fisheries, were gathering and distributing statistical information in order to meet their departmental or administrative necessities, so that at the

time this report was made nearly all of the provinces had more or less extended statistical branches at work upon, different lines of examination,, gathering and selecting and distributing information. There "were three or four different bodies gathering statistics on crop reports, for instance, and agricultural production, doing the work separately, province iby province, and not having the same basis for their questionings, different results were obtained, and it became very difficult indeed to place authoritative reliance upon the statistics as they were gathered, in so far as they affected the Dominion as a whole. The Dominion was also preparing crop reports and making returns of agricultural production, and there was a difference in method between the Dominion Government and the provincial governments. In consequence, not only was there overlapping, but a condition of things came about in which the outside world, and in fact the people of Canada, did not know on which set of statistics to rely.
The outside world was in doubt as to what was authoritative, and it also had its contradictions within the Dominion itself. As soon as the commission's report was made, steps were taken in Canada to work it out along the lines of the principles laid down for organization by the commission. In the first place, conferences were held between the Dominion Statistical Branch, and the statistical branches of the various provinces; Mr. Grigg, in his time, travelled from one end of the country to the other, and had conferences with the different statistical branches of the provinces, and they canvassed the whole question, and came to certain conclusions as to agreement and co-operation. That resulted in calling a Dominion conference of the statistical heads representing the provincal and Dominion authorities. At that conference, statistical methods, in so far as they affect the pi-ovinces and the Dominion, were canvassed, and certain agreements were come to. These were to be worked out by the central statistics, office here, and afterwards to -be submitted to the provincial authorities, which has been done. Again, in 1915, on the demise of Mr. Blue, Mr. Coats, from the Department of Labour, was appointed Dominion statistician and he took up the work as he found it at that time, and proceeded with it upon the same lines. Since then the endeavour lias been to co-ordinate the work in the departments at Ottawa that were gathering statistics, to prevent overlapping, to get uniformity,
to secure the best method, and to ensure as great economy of working as possible. On the other hand, the same system of conference and co-operation- was carried out, with reference to the provincial authorities, and at the present time I may say, with reference to all the branches of statistical information, selection and distribution, that there is complete accord and harmony between the Dominion statistical office and the statistical offices of the different provinces. Where the provincial organization is ap-paiently the most reliable for gaining the information, it is availed of. Where the Dominion plan or organization appears more reliable, that plan is adopted. There is agreement on both these points a-s to the selection and tabulation of the information. In nearly all cases the tabulation is done in the Dominion statistical office, where we have the greatest facilities for doing it, and the information, when tabulated, is returned again for the use of the agricultural and other statistical departments of the provincial governments, whilst of course the same information remains with the statistical office here in Ottawa. These have been the lines along which the Dominion statistician -has been working, with the results I have jus-t mentioned. It is proposed to call this a bureau rather than a statistical office, because the word bureau widens the meaning somewhat, and is more in accord with similar institutions in other countries. The main idea is that, so far as the gathering of general or economic statistics is concerned, it shall be the work of the bureau itself, but departmental statistics for administrative purposes remain with the departments. In so far as, by co-operation, mutual advice and direction, the -gathering of the -statistics in the administrative departments can he mffde -to fi-t in with the general plan, and can conduce to economy and accuracy of selection, that co-operation and co-ordination takes place' between the central office and the statistical branches of the different departments working along their lines of administrative records- and statistics.
With regard to what has been accomplished, the Dominion statistician and his higher staff in that office have been making a series of very thorough investigations and examinations and have been laying out the field for a general statistical operation. It might be interesting to the House, if I were to briefly mention the different fields or divisions of work that are now being prepared for, and which have been or will be put into operation.

In the first place, we keep our old decennial census. We have each ten years been taking the census of the Dominion, with the collateral information, outside of statistics of population, which has been gathered hitherto and which may be easily gathered in a census of population. Agriculture and population go together in the schedules which result in the information gathered in the decennial census.

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext: Will those last figures be quoted in the agricultural reports, or will they appear in the Year Book?

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext:
I have spoken of the decennial census of population and agriculture, but it has long been felt in this country, and in this House, that a ten-year census of the condition, or the situation as regards agriculture is not quite sufficient for these times through which we are passing. Therefore, in addition to the decennial census of population and agriculture, it is proposed to add an annual census of livestock and crops, the record of marketing, and the statistics of butter and cheese production, so that each year we shall have an up-to-date statement as regards the condition of agricultural work, so far as that can be interpreted by statistics, which will supplement the information which is got in the decennial census with regard to agriculture itself. We have been having a kind of crop report, but it was not very widely based, and consequently has not included sufficient information to enable reliable estimates to be made. The idea underlying this yearly census is to develop the sources of information, t-o distribute more widely the area of information upon which we draw, and to make the estimates approximate, as nearly as possible, to the actualities of the case. In June, our crop reporters, who were selected and distributed throughout the country, gave us a statement as to the areas under cultivation, the crops sown and the number of live stock. These were followed up in the succeeding months by reports upon the condition of the crops, the live stock, and the like of that. The wider you can get the basis of the information upon which you can apply your final estimate, the more reliable the result will be. That is where co-operation is taking place between the Dominion and the provinces. I do not know that I can do better than just read an extract from the plan to show the improvement that has been made and the benefit that will arise therefrom:
As to the crops and livestock the statistics are issued monthly, the basic data relating to crops and numbers of live stock are obtained in

June on a card designed to reach every farmer in Canada.
A specimen card is appended here and can be seen by any hon. member who desires.
The specimen card is issued in co-operation with the provincial departments of agriculture. The arrangements for co-operation differs slightly in the oase of each province. For example, In the case of the provinces of Quebec, Saskatchewan and Alberta, the cards are distributed and collected by .the provincial authorities through the rural school teachers and then returned to this office for compilation.
By the co-operation of the educational authorities in these provinces, the teachers, in the first place, are prepared by an instructional circular which is issued to them for the kind of work which they are expected to facilitate. Then this card, prepared by the central office here, is sent out and approved of. The card is made out after consultation between the provincial authorities and our statistical office. These cards are then sent out to the departments in the three provinces. These departments, through the educational branches of the governments, forward these cards to the school teachers in every district. The cards are then distributed by the scholars and brought back to the teacher, a lesson having been given to the scholars in the meantime as to the significance of this operation and as to the public service involved, and as a result they are interested in it. These cards are then brought back by the children, are sent in to the provincial authorities, and by these are forwarded for compilation purposes to the central office.
In British Columbia' the cards are mailed by this office to individual farmers and returned to the provincial department for compilation. British Columbia has had a system of sending direct to farmers a form that is the basis of estimates as to' crops. They consider that the best way of doing it and they are doing it in that way rather than through the teachers. Ontario and Manitoba this year are coming in practically on the same basis as British Columbia. The details are already settled. The Maritime Provinces have agreed to the principle of co-operation ,and the details are to be arranged during the present month. It is interesting to note the results for 1917 in the case of Quebec, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. In Quebec returns have been received from 29,000 farmers; in Saskatchewan from 35,000; in Alberta from 14,500, and in British Columbia from 6,900.

Under the old system of crop reporters we had only an infinitesimal fraction of that number; consequently, our basis was that much curtailed. Here the basis upon which the estimates are to be formed from the whole country is widened very largely.
Passing from the census Oif population and of agricultural production, with the addition of the annual statistics gathered, to keep up to date between the decennial periods, we take up the next division; that is, the census of production. We propose to do for industrial production, taken in its widest sense, what has hitherto been done with regard to agricultural production and population. Hitherto all we have got in respect to industrial production has been what we have been able to gather at the decennial census. In addition to the difficulty of getting an adequate industrial census by means of the schedules which are distributed for the decennial census, and which must include so much other matter, we had no further information for each of the nine years intervening (between decennial periods. That is not what is necessary in these days and particularly in the face of Canada's largely increased and increasing industrial activity. What it is proposed to do is to take in each ten years a general census of industrial production, taking it in a different period from that at which the decennial census of agriculture and population is taken and then basing upon that, just the same as is done in the case of the agricultural census, a postal census of the industrial production each year, to keep up to date, in so far as it can be done, with the progress that is being made in our industrial activities. We shall be doing for .industrial production in this respect what is done for agriculture an the other division.
In that there will be combined fishing, mining, lumbering, forestry, manufacturing-all the great basic indhstries of Canada. One will see how necessary that is when it is stated that some twenty-nine departments, under Dominion work and under provincial work, have been publishing statistics of production during the last number of years with all their different methods, in a fragmentary manner more or less, and without uniformity or co-ordination. Between all these departments and the central statistical office there is now a plan of co-operation; each taking its own part in a co-ordinated plan, and all working together for the general result, which I anticipate will be excellent.
The third division takes in statistics of trade and of commerce. At present these statistics are under the management of the Customs Department, the Trade and Commerce Department, and the Statistical Department-three departments. What is proposed in respect of these is, by co-operation and co-ordination to prevent overlapping between these three departments; to hit upon and carry out a system which shall be carried on with the greatest economy and with the greatest efficiency, and without one department overlapping in any respect the work which is being done by the other.
Then there is the division of transportation, which, of course, is intimately connected with production-with natural production and industrial production-and the statistics with reference to which are absolutely necessary if we shall come to any correct interpretation of the forces at work in Canada contributing to the business and trade and national prosperity of the country.
Vital statistics are also to be taken up in a new and adequate way. Up to the present time vital statistics have been chiefly gathered by the provinces. Some provinces have none; some provinces have more or less well developed plans. Complete accord has been reached between the statistical office here and the vital statistics branches of the different province^, and a plan of gathering and distributing these vital statistics has been arranged for and will now be carried out. Members will see how vital this is to our country, as it is considered vital to all progressive countries. There has been a great lack of complete vital statistics in this country up to the present time, and we now propose to have that lack remedied.
Criminal statistics are being gathered in a way, and have been for a number of years, but I do mioit think any one will contend that they have been satisfactory; they have not been broad or thorough enough. The gathering of criminal statistics will be enlarged .and carried out, I hope, with greater advantage to the country at large.'

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext: Enlarged in what way?

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext:
Well, for instance, that there will be a wider range .selected. Criminal statistics are published in part; we have a publication of our own on criminal statistics. Several oif the provincial governments have also statistics, more or less, that they are gathering. These will

be enlarged to take in all that is necessary for a well founded system of criminal statistics, and then all will be brought together and published, or distributed, in a form in which you will get everything that i.s vital to the understanding of the subject, instead of having to rummage round through the different provinces, .and here in the Dominion, to gather the information and pick it out from these different sources.
Then there is the division of wealth, and debt, and taxation, which will take in governmental, municipal, corporation, and private finance. Not very much attention has been given to the collation and coordination of such material as already exists, 'but which exists without being put [DOT]in a form where it can toe readily of use. The Union of Municipalities has been very insistent upon the improvement, or the creation, of a system of statistics for the Dominion which shall aid them in their municipal work; and with the co-ordination of the municipal authorities, the provincial authorities and ourselves, it is proposed to enlarge that system of gathering statistics, and to collate it in a form where it can be easily got at and be readily usable.

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext: Would the minister give an example as to what he intends doing, for instance, toy the collation of municipal statistics?

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext: I think my hon. friend knows that pretty nearly as well as I do myself. All our municipalities govern themselves-. They have their system of expenditures and of revenues; they have their debts and their tax systems, everything of that kind, and each municipality knows what it itself is doing, and it knows to a certain extent the plans along which it is working, but there is no collation of this for the municipalities as a whole, and tUffere-fore for the Dominion as a whole.

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext:
I understand. It will
simply be the embodying of the yearly financial statements of the municipalities.

maintopic: DOMINION BUREAU OF STATISTICS.
speechtext:
It will be that, but it will also be something more, because the moment you begin to do that and to show the different systems which are at work in one municipality and another, it gives a chance for a comparison which is not feasible when the operations of each municipality in its own department appears alone.
All I have to state in addition to what I have already said deals with the editorial and publishing phases of these general statistics. We have, as hon. gentlemen

know, a Year Book, which was instituted in 1886, and which has been improved from-year to year, until to-day I think I can say that Canada has a Year Book which it is not ashamed to let go out into any country in the world. We have had from other countries, I may say, very strong commendations, and expressions of approval as>
to the Year Book as it is now published. The publications, of course, will take in matter which is gathered in any of these different divisions with such annotations and analyses of them as it is really the highest work of the statistical office to accord in connection with facts once they are gathered.
I have troubled the House a little longer than I had anticipated, but I have been under the impression that probably not enough attention was given to the importance of statistical work in our country, and that not as much attention has been given to it as ought to be given to it in this House. Everybody will admit that a system of broad, well-based, accurate information running out into all the possible sources of activity of our country is not only a good, but an absolutely necessary thing to have in these days. Everything we do-I mean morally, spiritually to a certain extent, and to an absolute extent in the way of business, trade and finance is based upon facts. Facts constitute the foundation upon which they are to be based if results are to be satisfactory.
All our activities more or less demand a foundation of accurate and particular information. Not only do we need that for our country and1 its own business, but we are side toy side with the progressive countries of the world, whose statistical systems during the last ten or fifteen years have been wonderfully improved, and if Canada is to do her work and perform her part in the world of nations, she must have a statistical system, which, soi far as possible, will not only be adequate to her needs, but which will bear comparison with that of other nations and be for the benefit of the country in its relations with other countries. I do not think it is necessary for me to say anything more as an introduction to the Bill.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivini in the Chair.
On section 3-Dominion Bureau of Statistics.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways and Canals) Bill 51, to provide compensation where employees of His Majesty are killed or suffer injuries while performing their duties was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1, subsection 1-compensation to be same as under law of province where accident occurs.
Mr. iCURRJE: In Ontario there may be [DOT]i liability on the part of some of the railways coming under the operation of the Government, and a boiard has been created which takes the place of workmen's compensation legislation in that province. Is, it the intention of the Government to contribute to the funds of that board? The Ontario Government have done away with the old Employers' Liability Act, and a department of the government deals with this question. Every employer pays so much money into this fund annually. No doubt the railways will be taken over shortly, and there is a large mileage of railway in Ontario. Has the minister considered the operation of the compensation

8 lil
board in Ontario, or will this clause cover the whole thing?
iMr. J. D. RElIiD: The intention of this Bill is to bring not only the railways but all Government employees on public works under a compensation Act. I may say, the railway employees prefer the Dominion Act, but it takes some time to work it out, and therefore I am introducing this Bill and placing all the employees in exactly the same position as the employees ot a private railway. The Bill has been framed on that basis. The hon. gentleman asks whether it is the intention of the Government to deposit an amount with the Ontario Government, under the laws of that province. I may say it is not necessary for the Government of Canada to deposit any amount to ensure that any judgment under that Compensation Act will be paid. I do not know whether the law compels the Canadian Pacific or Canadian Northern to deposit any money, but it is not the intention of the Government to do so. In case of accident, injury or death, any liabilities will be paid in accordance with the amount the employees would bo entitled to in any province.
Mr. CURRIE;,. The Ontario Government's officers will assess the damages to the person injured, and this Government'will pay it?	*

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The court, or whatever the tribunal is.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: There is a board?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Yes. The Dominion Government Railways will go through the same procedure as the Canadian Pacific, in case one of their employees is injured.
Mr. 'COPP: Has the substance of this Bill been submitted t-o representatives of the labour organizations on the Canadian Government railways for their approval?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Yes, we have discussed it with some gentlemen representing some of the organizations. There is a clause referring to the provident fund, and it was with some of those connected with that fund we discussed it. The employees on the Intercolonial railway are satisfied, because they have this additional security.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
The last line or two of this subsection says:
-shall be determined in the same manner and by the same 'board, officers or authority or by suelh other board, officers or authority, or by such court as the Governor in Council shall from time to time direct.
Why is it necessary to establish another court? Why take it out of the hands of the regular courts?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: As I understand the provision of the clause, its purpose is to enable us to follow the law that exists in each province. I suppose the hon. gentleman wishes to know why it is necessary to appoint any board by Order in Council?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I understand that in Prince Edward Island, for instance, they have no board of arbitration, and no law such as we have in Ontario, and it might be necessary to appoint some board in that province similar to the boards in other provinces. That is the reason that clause was inserted.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The province of Ontario has a compensation board, with a staff of officials; and manufacturers, or others employing over a certain number of persons come under the regulations of that board. There is a certain expense every year which those who come under that board have to pay into the treasury for the maintenance of that board and to pay its inspectors and officers. I should think it would be advisable, if the Government railways come under the operation of that board, that they should pay a certain amount into that fund annually, the same as any one else. It would not be fair to have an irganizu-tion work for the Dominion Government for nothing, because this service examines into these cases, and sends its inspectors to various points. When the award is made the Government will pay the award but it will not pay any of the expenses of the men who have gone out to investigate. I do not know whether the Bill makes any provision that out of the consolidated revenue fund there should be any payment besides the award that is paid to the person injured.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Is this Bill to be made retroactive?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: It is not retroactive.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Take the case of employees on a gravel train, or in a sand pit, and working for His Majesty the King, who are insured against accident for an amount of $250. If some of them sustain injuries are they entitled to compensation under this Act? It seems that parties who are injured cannot put in any claim for damages beyond the amount for which they are insured. I remember a case in my own

constituency where a man had his two legs broken. I made an appeal to the solicitor of the Intercolonial railway at Moncton and he told me that the Government was not responsible beyond the amount of $250. I ask the minister whether or not this man by signing an agreement can prefer any other claim beyond $25?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Perhaps I might venture to answer the - question of the hon. member (Mr. Michaud). If the party injured is an employee of the Government railway, he is entitled to just the same remedy, and subject to just the same restrictions, should this Act pass as if he was employed on an ordinary railway. The law of the province applies in just the same way as it would if he were employed on another railway. In the other case the hon. gentleman brings forward, if under the law of the province in which the man resides, an insurance fund would be deducted from any amount he might otherwise receive, or would not be deducted, it would be deducted or not deducted according 'to his agreement. That would be the result in an action where the party was employed in the Government railway. I think that is clear.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Under the present law, is that young man entitled to any compensation from the Government outside of his $250 insurance?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean by " present law ''-Dominion law or provincial law?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The present Dominion law. He cannot come under the provincial law if he is working for a Government railway.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Under the present law, if I understand it-I may he wrong-compensation is paid by the Crown as an act of grace. There is no law governing the exact amount that shall be paid. This Bill establishes the principle of liability under the provincial law of the province where the man resides.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I understood from the solicitor of the Intercolonial railway at Moncton that His Majesty is not responsible for any accident to any of his employees. Is that right?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Therefore, a widow and children cannot bring action against the Government for the death of the husband and father?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: No. This Bill, however, makes it possible for them to get compensation. In the hon. gentleman's province, in case of an accident on the -Canadian Pacific railway, they can bring action against the company under the Compensation Act and get damages. But they could not do that if the accident happened on the Government railway. This now puts the Government railway in the same position in that province as the Canadian Pacific would be. In case of injury, an employee of the Government railway will be in exactly the same position in regard to compensation as would the employee of a railway company.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I am afraid that this Bill constitutes an encroachment on provincial rights. I see the minister smiling, but that is the construction I put on section 1. It says that the amount of compensation shall be determined by-
-the same Board1, officers or authority, or by such other board, officers or authority or by such court as the Governor In Council shall from time to time direct.
I understand that if there is no board, officers or authority, or any court, the Governor in Council may appoint a board, officers, or authority to deal with these cases. Why not make this clause clear, so that there will be no misunderstanding? Make . it read:
Such compensation shall be determined in the same manner and by the same board, officers or authority, if any, or, if none, by such other hoard, officers or authority as the Governor in Council Shall appoint.
My opinion is that in a province where there is already authority constituted the Governor in Council, under this clause, can appoint another authority.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: It is very clear now.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I beg the hon. minister to listen. To make my point very clear:
I am always afraid of the explanations given by the hon. minister. When we were discussing the Military Service Bill he told the House that the province of Quebec should not be agitated by it because it would be the least affected; now the province of Quebec ie supposed to be the most affected.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I am afraid my words
in that regard were only too true, but at present we are not discussing the Military Service Bill. I hope I may be as well within the mark now as I was on the occasion to which the hon. gentleman has referred What the hon. gentleman argues for is this: That the Governor in- Council should not take the power to establish a board which would have the determination of, and the application of, a provincial law in fixing this amount. But even though we do take this power, I was pointing out we, do not encroach upon any provincial right, because there is no- provincial right to encroach u-pon. I submit that we ought to take the power for the following reasons: The principle objection that could be raised against the Dominion putting itself in this position is that it places itself within the power of a province to establish a board over which the Dominion -has no control whatsoever, and no right to interfere with it in any way whatever, and enables that board to assess against the Crown in the right of the Dominion -such compensation as may seem fit. Now it was thought right that the Government place itself under the same principles as apply to the province, that we should- have the power to determine the nature of the tribunal which would apply those principles and assess the damages against the Crown. As the Minister of Railways has pointed out, there seems to be a special need of the exercise of that power now in Ithe province of Prince Edward Island, and there may be need of it elsewhere. It may be thought fit to order that in all cases of -claims against
the Crown in the right of the Dominion a superior court should exercise jurisdiction, or it m-ay be thought -fit to establish in each province a board which, applying the law of the province, would determine what the amount should be. It -seems to me only just that that right should be reserved inasmuch as we go to the extent of putting it within the power of a province to fix the principles and the law upon which we must pay damages.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Might I ask the Minister of the Interior (iMr. Meighen) for -a little more light on this subject? My reason for doing so is that I pledged myself to the railway men of my riding that I would see to it, as far as I -could, that such legislation as was in thei-r interest should be passed. In the constituency of Port Arthur we have the three transcontinental railways and nine divisional points where the engines and the crews are changed. Those railway men are the civil soldiers of the country, and they should receive, not any greater consideration, but as great consideration -as any other class in the community now receives. 'To-day they are labouring under two or three disabilities, and I have promised to use my influence to remove those disabilities. This is one of them; the employees on -Government railways are asking to receive the same rights and the same amount of compensation for injury given to the employees of -any other railway. If we do not establish that principle the result is going to be that we shall lose the good men in the railway service to the other railway systems that are not owned and operated by the Government. I have heard them -say that if they cannot get the same rights and protection as other railway em-ployees they would- go to work, for the Canadian Pacific railway, for instance, where they would -enjoy those rights, They want the Government railways not operated politically but operated by a commission absolutely divorced from politics, so that a man may rise by merit and merit only. II have pledged myself to do what I can to bring about that result.
A third matter I wish to bring up is that the railway men want the right to vote on election day so that if they are going out on duty they can come in and vote just as -soldiers were able to vote at the	last election.
These men have to get up at four or five o'clock -in -the morning, or earlier, to -attend to their duties, and cannot record their votes because they are off guarding His Majesty's mail, or carrying food and war supplies, -and so forth, in doing which

they are discharging their duty to the country. These three grievances the railway men want remedied, and I iseek to enlist the sympathy and support of this House on their behalf for that .purpose.
Now, as regards this section, the Minister of the Interior has explained, if I understand it aright, that it is desired in- some way to keep control over the provincial legislature in the way of how ,it may legislate. If I understand the position correctly it is this: First of all there is the principle of law that the Crown is not liable in any action by any suppliant without its permission, which is the well-known and right principle. Now we are making an inroad into that principle by this legislation, and nightly making it. Then the principle as to liability, as I understand it, is, that if the province has not Workmen's Compensation Boards, and so forth, there is a common law liability, under a well known and celebrated case that every lawyer knows, by which if a man is engaged in a hazardous undertaking he is entitled to recover damages, which damages must be reasonable in amount. Under the provincial law, as I take it-the Minister of the Interior will correct me if I am wrong,

any court in a province where they have not these workmen's compensation- boards, would decide the -matter upon the -principle of common law. Now, is the railway man in any way to fee deprived first of all of his right undeT the common law where there is no- board or tribunal, or otherwise? Or iis he entitled to go- to the tribunals of the land-or in case of his demise, have his widow and children -that right-and sue for damages, thus being put in the same position as any other railway employee? That is the point I want to make cle-ar beyond possibility of doubt. If that were not iso, and there was not the common law liability, then the Grown might want to -step in and create -some tribunal, but it would be only in case, I should think, where the common law liability is not retained; otherwise I should think it would be -a dangerous proceeding to leave the matter entirely in the hands of the Cro-wn to step in and constitute a special tribunal. I would like that point m-ade clear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman to ask whether or not the former common law liability will be retained.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: There was no former common law liability as against the Crown.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I mean the same common law that applies to other subjects,

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: There is no common law liability now against the Crown. But I would say that the common law liability as it exists in any province as applied to a railway corporation may now, if this Bill passes, be utilized against the Crown, and will be in effect unless it has been displaced by provincial legislation.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That is perfectly clear.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I endorse what has just been said by the hon. member from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer) as to the importance of and necessity for this legislation.
There is certainly no reason why the State should not be treated or considered as an ordinary employer of labour. I know of many injustices which have been done to workmen on the Intercolonial railway because of the lack of such legislation. The other day, when the resolution which preceded this Bill was discussed in committee, I enquired whether there were Workmen's Compensation Acts in all the provinces, and I was told -that there was such legislation in all the provinces. A gentleman well posted on labour questions has told me that there are several provinces where no such legislation exists. If the hon. minister has the information as to that he should supply it to his colleague, the Minister of Labour, because I hold in my hand -a pamphlet issued by the Labour Department last year entitled *' Labour Legislation in -Canada," and I read this:
In 1916 laws in the field of labour legist lation were passed by the Federal Government and by the legislatures of all the provinces except Prince Edward Island. The outstanding feature was tihe enactment of workmen's compensation laws in the provinces of Manitoba and British Columbia, following the passage of compensation statutes in Ontario in 1914 and in Nova Scotia in 1915. In the autumn of 1915 the British Columbia Government appointed a commission to investigate the subject of workmen's compensation, which reported favourably in time for tihe passage of th-e Act at the next session of the legislature. The enactment of modern compensation laws by four provinces brings Canada fairly well in line with the rapid development of legislation of this kind throughout the world.
This would indicate that as far as th-e Labour Department is concerned they are not informed as to whether such legislation exists in all the provinces of the Dominion. On the other hand, the information given there is certainly incomplete, because I know, as a matter of fact, that in the prov-

ince of Quebec a compensation law was enacted in 1909, the first labour compensation legislation in the Dominion of Canada. ,If the province of Quebec comes last on woman's suffrage, it was the pioneer as far as labour legislation is concerned. So, if the information .of the Department of Labour was wrong as to Quebec, it may have been wrong for the other provinces as well. I would like to know, and the Committee is entitled to the information, whether such legislation exists in all the provinces?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I do not think the hon. gentleman realizes what the compensation laws of these provinces mean. In the provinces generally, under the common law, I think a man could bind 'himise'lf outside of compensation. That is, I could hire a man and make an agreement with him under the common law that if he sustained any injury he or his iheins could not ask for any compensation.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That is not good law.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Then there was another law passed in England-I think it was called Lord Campbell's Act

the lawyers in the House will correct me if I am in error, because I do not speak as a lawyer but as am employer of labour

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: You are not talking good law.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
However, there was a law passed there which made it so that .a man could not contract outside of the operation of securing compensation. Supposing a man was killed, his family could sue regardless of any agreement made with the employer. That is the British law. Now, all the provinces passed statute laws of that character, and the law the hon. gentleman refers to in Quebec is along that line. In the province of Ontario the insuring of the employee is taken entirely out of the bands of the employers, and a board is set up which insures every workman who seeks employment with a corporation or individual, and if he is killed or injured, the Government has a number of inspectors who visit the man or the place bf hiis employment and take all the evidence in the case, and the workmen's compensation board at Toronto fixes the degree of liability -and the compensation, whether it is to 'be an annual payment extending over the lifetime of the widow, and sio on. They fix it, and the Government pays it, and they charge that up generally to every business or employment in the category. All kinds of businesses
are categorized. For instance, munitions is in category C; farming will be category A, -and so on, -all the way down the line, and the compensation is in accordance with the category; but practically' the amount paid into this fund annually is in accordance with the risk. I might say in that connection that in the province of Ontario in the year 1916 in a munitions plant that I know of the premium was something like $350. Previous to that the amount paid to the insurance companies would run about six or seven hundred dollars. So we find the Compensation Act works a great reduction in the cost of carrying the risk of the workmen. Previously, the workmen could get practically nothing at all. The employer paid into a liability company, which employed every lawyer it could get to keep the workman from securing damages, and their whole business was to prevent him from obtaining damages. They stood behind the manufacturer and said: If you incur any damages, we will pay them, but we will put the workman and his wife and children through all the courts in the land before they will he able to collect anything from you. That was a vicious principle in itself. Now, these hoards fix the compensation. But. like the high cost of living and everything else, the amount paid into the province of Ontario last year as premiums increased three hundred per cent over the previous year, and there is a great deal of grumbling about that. It .is claimed that the board has assessed the figure for the year far too high in order to accumulate a large fund for itself. In the province of Quebec, I think there is not a board of that description; I understand there is not. But the province of British Columbia has adopted the principle, having largely copied from the law of the State of Washington. The other provinces down by the sea have also adopted a similar .-system; it is a splendid system for both employer and workman. But unless boards are established, I think the law will -stand1, not the old common law, but the general law of all the provinces, that a man cannot contract himself out of his right of claim upon his employer in case he is injured. Under the old common law he could not do that, it being held that he was a free agent.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
.If it is intended that the law of the province with respect to the amount of compensation and the manner of obtaining it is to govern, the section as it now stands is a little obscure. The wording of the clause is as follows:

-and the liability for and the amount of such compensation ghall he determined in the same manner and by the same Board, officers or authority, or by such other Board, officers or authority or by such court as the Governor in Council shall from time to time direct.
If we out out the alternative clause, it will read as follows:

and the liability for and the amount of such compensation shall be determined in the same manner and by the same Board, officers or authority, as the Governor in Council shall from time to time direct.
There are no similar actions at all, because it is within the authority of the Governor in Council absolutely to determine the (board. I would suggest that the clause he amended in this manner:
-and the liability for and -the amount of such compensation shall be determined in the same manner and by the same Board, officers or authority, as similar actions for compensation are determined under the laws of such province, or by such other Board, officers of authority or by such oourt as the Governor in Council shall from time to ' time direct.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Striking the alternative out?

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: No, there is no alternative. As it reads now, the section says: " shall be determined by the same board as the Governor in Council shall direct." I suggest that after the word " authority," in the third line from the last, there be added the words-: " as similar claims for compensation are determined under the laws of such province." Then, if in any particular province there is no board for the purpose of determining compensation the alternative clause will apply and the Governor in Council may appoint such authority as is deemed expedient.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The parliamentary counsel, our railway solicitor, and, I think, the Chairman of the Railway Commission, all assisted in drafting this clause with a view to having it right.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: In the multitude of counsel there is wisdom.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: My whole object is to get this Bill in such shape that in cases of accident employees on Government railways shall have the same rights as employees of other railways. Under the present law, if a man is injured or killed, I have no way of providing compensation for his family. Cases have been dealt with in the estimates, but it is not fair to me or to the family that I should have to decide the matter in that way.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Does this not mean that the minister, the Government, or the de-
[Mr. Middlebro.J
partment desires to put itself, in every province, in the position of a private corporation, and then to come under the operations of the compensation law of that province?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That is what I have in view.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That is an object with which we can all sympathize. My hon. friend has had half a dozen lawyers preparing this clause, and it must be right, I suppose. The object is certainly a worthy one, but I should not gather it from the reading of the clause as it stands.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Suppose that during the course of his employment a 9 p.m. man receives an injury which does not come within the terms of the Compensation Ac,t, and the compensation board in the particular province refuses to take jurisdiction over him, what remedy i-s open to the dependents of that man-? 'Mr. MEIGHEN: That is -my understanding.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: If that is a correct interpretation of the Act, the provision is an excellent one.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: In view of the suggestions which have been made, the law clerk should he asked to go over this -section very carefully. While the marginal notation may read all right, I confess that a few more words seem to ibe necessary in order to make the clause absolutely clear.

speechtext: In that case, what harm would there be in adding after the amendment just moved by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), that in case no such board of officers exists in the province, or in the absence of any compensation law in force in the province, the Governor in Council may determine before what board or court the injured person may come?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I endeavoured to state the point of view of the Government before. We do not wish to take the authority and apply it only in cases where there is no provincial law so as to fix Dominion lia-right to establish a tribunal in any case that we see fit, or in all cases that we see fit. The distance Parliament is going to in placing it within the power of the province to establish the laws and the principles upon which we shall pay damages seems to me to be a long way indeed, without asking us to go the further length of placing ourselves wholly within the jurisdiction of such tribunal, of whatever character, as the province may establish for applying that law and determining the amount of compensation. It may be that in no case except
fi2
where there is no tribunal, shall we exercise that right, but we wish to reserve it, and it might be that the Governor in Council might see fit to enact that only a Superior Court in any province should apply the provincial law so as to fix Dominion liability.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I entirely agree with what was said a few moments ago by my hon. friend from Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer). He asked the Government to put the railway man working for the Government in exactly the same position as the ordinary man.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: As to law.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
That was his idea, if I understood -him correctly. But this goes further. Supposing a man gets injured while working on a Government steamer or on a public work; under this Act he would be entitled- to compensation, whether he was working for the Minister of Customs, the Minister of Railways, or the Minister of Public Works. My hon. friend said he was afraid it might not be the judge of a Superior Court who would take cognizance of the case. I suppose it is the same in other provinces as in Quebec, where the jurisdiction of the judge is limited by the amount involved. In our province it is -specifically provided that it is the judge of the Superior Court who shall take original cognizance of the case. Before an injured man can sue, he has to present a petition, and when that petition is presented, if employer and employee agree the judge renders judgment which has the same effect as if the action had been tried by the court in the regular way. I am not speaking on behalf of my district particularly, because we have no Government railways. I had forgotten; we have the Canadian Northern paid for by the Government, but not yet owned or operated *by the Government. Under this legislation, -thle railwayman working for the Government would not feel they were on the same footing as the men'working for the -Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk, -because there wo-uld always be an uncertainty as to the Government creating a board to decide these compensation " cases. -But knowing the sympathy of the Minister of Railways for the working man,
I do not think he would make any change which would be to their disadvantage; but we know he does change his mind- sometimes, and we have precedents enough for that if we look backward.



There is -another point. Would it not be well to mention in the Bill that the action may 'be brought against the department in which the injured man was employed? Because if the action is simply brought against His Majesty the King, we' should see His Majesty King George the Fifth summoning His Majesty King George the Fifth to appear before the Superior Court of Three Rivers or elsewhere to answer to John Doe, who has broken his leg" while in the employ of His Majesty. We might provide that when a man brings an action for personal injury, the fact of designating the department for which he was working will be sufficient to bring the Crown before the -court. T remember that when we amended the Railway Act to allow people to- bring claims up to $500 for cattle killed [DOT]by the railway, a special board was appointed and the action was brought against this board and that was sufficient to make the Crown -appear. The Crown has gone extensively into the railway business, and Government railways cover the whole country. Heretofore, Moncton has been the seat of railway operations by the Crown. In an action for damages, would the injured man have to serve notice on the minister or the deputy minister at Ottawa, or in the head office of the railway company, or in the resident engineer's office for the Department of Railways, or on the customs officer of the district if the accident happened to a man in the customs service? I think we should set out in the Bill who shall be sued when a man wants to sue the Crown for personal injury, and where the Crown may be served. Otherwise, if the labourer has to eerve the documents in Ottawa or at some divisional point he might be put to considerable expense. On the Canadian Pacific, if an accident occurs, the injured man may serve the head office in Montreal or the agent at the place where the accident happened. Perhaps the minister would draft a paragraph errftiodying my suggestions.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I think the principle
of this Bill is an excellent one, and I am certainly in favour of the Crown granting compensation -to employees suffering in* juries through the operation of the railways. I think this is the natural corollary of the legislation passed some years ago by which those who suffered from fires caused by sparks from -an engine on the Intercolonial could sue to the amount of $200 before the courts of the province through which the train passed. I do not think the paragraph before us is quite clear. The Government

first of all admits the jurisdiction of the courts of the provinces to adjudicate these cases, and accepts the various compensation Acts passed by the different provinces. The courts of the provinces, although created by the provinces themselves, are paid out of the federal exchequer. As the Government by this legislation accepts the compensation Acts of the provinces why not trust the administration of this Act to the Superior Court judges of the provinces? Why does the Government take power to create special boards in the various provinces? The Government will accept the compensation Acts which are provided for by the different provinces; it seems invidious that it will not accept the jurisdiction of the courts in the provinces and pass the administration of that Act to those special boards. You are creating an invidious distinction as between our judges in the various provinces, who are paid by the federal exchequer although created by local legislatures, whilst you admit the validity and the scope of our Compensation Act. If the Government were providing for special boards which would administer compensation Acts differently from the provincial Acts, I could understand this legislation. I say to the Government; The legislation is excellent; the principle is most excellent, but I do not understand why you do not trust the provincial courts in the administration of the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: In the Constitution of this country the greatest care was observed in providing for the establishment and the manning of our courts. The balance was well preserved between Dominion and provincial responsibility, and if all the provinces had referred the administration of their compensation law to the courts, then I do not apprehend that this alternative would have been inserted in the Bill. But a board established purely under provincial law, and manned only by provincial authority, is not naturally a board in which the Dominion would be likely to place irrevocably its destiny in these matters; at all events in the isame way as we might be quite prepared to place it if the provincial law prescribed the court to adjudicate, instead of a board.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Why do you not limit it to provinces where they have no board?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
For the reason that the province itself has not limited it. The province comes along, displaces the jurisdiction of the court, and establishes a board, and we would have, by Order in

Council to re-establish the jurisdiction of the court and place our cases under their jurisdiction. Consequently we -musit take this alternative. Otherwise we are wholly within the power of a board constituted by provincial authority, manned by provincial authority, in respect of which this Dominion has no say whatever. My hon. friend asks: Why not at once remove the jurisdiction of boards, and place this wholly within the power of the Superior Court of each province? That might be done, but it was thought better to try it with the boards that now exist, and see how it operated, and what effect it would have. It is true they are in no way answerable to us, they are appointed by provincial authority, paid by provincial funds, and in no way in the nature of courts established under the provisions of the British North America Act. It might be well to try the operation of this law as administered by the 'board, but we retain power, not only to establish a .board, or a court where there is none now, but to displace the board now established, if we see fit, by a court or a board which may sit through all the provinces, as the Governor in Council may see fit.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
If I understand the position, we have now come down practically to what you might call a constitutional question, whether the Dominion of Canada shall or shall not be willing to submit itself, as far as this principle of liability is concerned, to the provincial courts. The hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. J. D. Reid) says: Yes, I want to see all the men employed in the Government railways receive the same treatment as men employed in any other railway. The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen), being a very able lawyer, and realizing much more fully the meaning of these words, practically says: No, I will only agree to the provincial authority, provided we are satisfied with it. Let us use blunt language in this matter; let us place the cards on the table. I think it would be a horrible mistake, when dealing with railway employees, to leave the matter in such a position that it could be argued in two or three ways. These men do not like to be deceived. I am a new member of the House, and do not know which is the proper course to adopt. They are both very far-reaching. It is a dangerous thing for the Federal Government to submit itself without reservation- to the provinces-. Canada stands to-day in a peculiar position in regard to railways. I hardly think any of us realize it. We are to-day the owners of -about 15,000 miles of
railway-the largest railway owner in Canada. We have seen fit, and rightly' s'o, to take over these railways. Having done so, and having come into competition with other existing railways, it seems to me that we ought to take the liabilities incident to taking over the railways. "Remember, these liabilities will be very far-reaching. We cannot stop at this matter. You have to take up the principle of municipal assessment later on, the principle of municipal liability for taxes, and so on, just as the railways have done. Heretofore the Government never allowed itself to be taxed, and rightly so. So that the matter cannot be disposed of very triflingly. It seems to me very unwise not to be able to say to the men: You are working on this railway for us; you are going to have exactly the same treatment as you would have working for any other railway. For that reason, I would like to see the Government s'o amend this clause that the principle would be clearly and well defined. It cuts into the principle that my hon. friend the hon. Minister of the Interior just enunciated. I should like to move an amendment-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: There is already an amendment before the Committee.

speechtext:
In order that the Committee may be considering it, I may say that the substance 'of my proposed amendment will be to insert after the word " or " in the 13th line the following:
[DOT]-if such board, officers or authority be not then existing.
That squarely defines the position, that if there is not an existing board, we will appoint one.
The -CHAIRMAN: The amendment now before the Committee is that proposed by the hon. Minister of the Interior.
Amendment agreed to on division.

When I moved my
amendment I had no thought of taking away the alternative from the Government. What the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) says is

quite sound, that we should give this Act a trial. say, give the present Act a trial and if it is satisfactory we do not need to change it. If it is not satisfactory, we can pass a new Act, as my hon. friend says.
(Mr. J. D. This Bill allows the Government to do that. I agree with the hon. member (Mr. Middlebro) who has just spoken. If some province should appoint a board, or adopt a law, by which the railway employees would not probably get as much as we believe they would be entitled to, we would be in a position to appoint a board that would see that they received their just dues.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: In that case we had better put it in the Bill.

This Bill has been
passed upon by the railway employees'. I would like to give it a trial, and if, by the *time another session, of Parliament is held, it does not work out as we expect, we can amend it. I think that to give away our powers in so far .as doing what is just and fair by the men is concerned would be to take a step that would hardly be justified.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
The minister started out with the very good intention of putting Government railway employees 'in the same position as the employees of any other railway. But, apparently the multitude of his legal advisors have got him into a bad plight

because he has-, by the first part of this section, given the employees of the Government railways what they are entitled to, but every man in this Parliament must realize that he leaves the hack door open, im the provision contained in the last line of the section, so that in case the award does not suit him he can withdraw the case from the board.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That is not so.

speechtext: That i'S as I understand it. I do not say that the minister intends to do that, hut that is 'actually how it works out. The provinces, apparently with one exception, have compensation Acts each 'administered by what are known as arbitration boards, as explained by the hon. member for North Si'mcoe (Mr. Currie) a few moments .ago-. A board as appointed by the provincial government to hear these cases, deliberate upon them and give their judgment the satisfaction of which becomes a charge upon the fund that has been raised by an 'assessment'upon these large corporations. The amendment moved fay the hon. *member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro) is all right 'as far as it goes, 'but the Canadian Government railway employees will not be satisfied with a clause which says that the Government, if not satisfied with the way in which the case has been tried before the arbitration board in the province in which the claimant resides, can fake it out of their -hands and appoint a board of their own. They may get just as good and just a reasonable a board, and a board that would give a fair judgment, but nevertheless the employees of the, Government railway will look upon it with a good deal of suspicion. 1 am absolutely an favour of the principle of this Bill, and I would like to see it adopted in such a shape that the Government would be protected as well as the employees of the road. But, this is how it will work out: Somebody is injured or killed on the Intercolonial railway and his dependents come Ihefore a hoard appointed by the legislature or government of the province of New Brunswick. The case proceeds, and the hO'ard, in the opinion of the minister, makes too large an allowance to the dependents.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I never made any such statement, and the hon. gentleman knows that I did not.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The ihon. gentleman is making 'out a case on supposition.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: No. Nothing of the kind.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Well, now, let us see.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Oh, no.

speechtext: For future cases.
