speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: You cann'ot do that with respect to future cases.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: You are changing your policy in that regard?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I think the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) understands the position. What would happen would he this: You must have a solicitor to look after the legal interests of the Department of _Railways and Canals, and the solicitor of the railway, who would be against the employee, would practically appoint the board that would sit upon the case and that would bring in its decision. I say that is absolutely contrary to the object of the Bill as explained by the Minister of Railways, when he told us that it was intended to put the employees of the Government railways on a fair and reasonable footing with the employees of all other railways and corporations. I agree with him that is the proper thing to do; but I protest in the strongest manner possible on behalf of the employees of the Intercolonial railway particularly, who are very numerous in the constituency which I represent, against taking power away from the hoards of the province of New Brunswick and placing it, in the hands of a board appointed by the Governor in Council, for that will raise suspicion in the minds of the railway employees which will be beneficial neither to the Government nor to the railway. If there is no compensation board in any province and you appoint a court to deal with the matter, well and good, but to give this power to a board to be appointed by the Governor in Council does not seem to be in the interests of the railway employees themselves or in the interests of the country.
Mr. 3. D. REID: The hon. member (Mr. Copp) is afraid that the railway employees
will not receive fair treatment if their case is tried by some tribunal appointed by the Dominion Government. Let me say to the hon. gentleman that a very large delegation of railway employees from all the different railway organizations came to Ottawa and urged me to bring in a Dominion Compensation Bill, and why? Because they claimed they were not getting fair treatment from some of the provincial boards.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: A permanent board?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The enactment of a Dominion Compensation Bill was what they wanted.	'	.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Exactly, providing for a permanent board.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: And my answer to the delegation was that we had not time during the present session to enact the legislation which they wanted, but that I would bring in a Compensation Bill that would fit in with the provincial laws for all the Dominion; and give it a trial, and at another session, if they so desired, I would be glad to introduce a Dominion Bill. Therefore, the railway employees were not only willing, but anxious, to trust their case in the hands of the Dominion Government. That is the stand they took within the last two weeks.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Then their faith is badly placed.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I do not agree with the hon. member. I am giving them my word that this Bill is intended to dovetail in with the provincial laws throughout the Dominion, and I ask hon. gentlemen to support the Bill as it is. Let us pass the Bill and give it a few months,' trial. Let it be tried until the next session of Parliament, and then if the railway employees say that the law is working out unsatisfactorily, let us do our best to perfect it. So far as I am concerned, my whole object is to try and secure the passage of a law that will be satisfactory to railway employees throughout the Dominion.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I can assure the minister
that the provision embodied in this section will not be satisfactory, but will be absolutely unsatisfactory to the railway men. It is unreasonable for one of the litigants interested in the case coming up for adjudication to have the right to appoint [DOT] the board. It would be just as reasonable,

I submit, to introduce an amendment providing that if the employees of the Government railway were not satisfied with the board appointed by the provincial government, or by my hon. friend opposite, they could apply for the appointment of an arbitration board of their own choosing. What ,ie fair for one ought to 'be fair for the other. The Minister of Railways may pass the Bill, but I tell him that within twenty-four hours after it is enacted and it goes down to employees of the (Intercolonial railway, and they realize what has been done, he will be flooded with protests against putting any such amendment on the statute-book. It is absolutely unjust towards the railway employees.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I think probably the
wisest thing to do in the interest of the railway men is to carry out the suggestion of the Minister of Railways. He has come down to the House in perfect good faith with legislation to better the railway men's condition. I welcome this Bill as an improvement on the existing law. It may not go quite as far as we would like it to go, indeed it is a sort of experiment, and I agree with the hon. member from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) that it would perhaps be better to compromise and accept the Bill just as it is with these amendments. Then if it does not work satisfactorily, and the House is so disposed, the law can be still further improved next session.

speechtext: The Minister of Railways made the statement that he had received a delegation representing not only the employees of the Government railways, but the employees of all the other railway systems.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Yes. As far as I can remember they represented all the different organizations of railway employees.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Did I understand the
minister to state that the delegation objected to the provincial boards and wanted a Dominion board appointed?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: No. What I stated was that a delegation of railway employees called on me and asked that a Dominion Compensation Bill be enacted, in other words, that the Compensation Act should apply to the same extent in one part of the Dominion as in another.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I am not asking questions from captious motives, I simply want information.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Yes, I recognize that. To put it in another way. What the railway employees submitted was something like this. The delegation stated that the law should be similar in character in every part of the Dominion. I informed them that as the session was likely to be short I could* not put such <a Bill through, but that I would introduce a Bill under which the employees of the Government railways would have identically the same rights as the employees of other railways enjoyed. Now, so far as I am concerned, if any employee of the Government railways, between now and the next session of Parliament, should be injured or killed, the claim for compensation would be treated in exactly the same manner as it would be if the employee belonged to the Canadian Pacific railway. maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: J wish to say-

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I will not take up the time of the committee to any great extent. I merely rise to offer a suggestion that I think would simplify the matter very materially. I cannot see any reason why matters of this kind should not be dealt with through the civil courts. I understand that such matters are dealt with through the civil courts in the province of Queibec. I am not a lawyer-and I may say in passing that I am glad of that seeing that lawyers are getting things mixed up so much. I am sorry for the Minister of Railways in that respect; I think he would have been well advised to have kept out of that. I am an ordinary business man, and my suggestion is that it would simplify matters if cases of this kind could be dealt with by the civil courts in all the provinces alike.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the discussion on this Bill has proceeded largely on the assumption that it is confined largely

to railway employees. It covers every man in the service of the Dominion Government, whether he is working on a railway, or a public building, or a dredge, or in any other capacity.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: It covers women too.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Yes, women as well.
Now, a suggestion has (been made that it would foe right and proper to leave this matter to the constituted courts in the various provinces. The legislature of Ontario, for instance, in their wisdom, have said that these are not matters that ought to be disposed of by courts. They have said; that any claim arising in that province ought to be determined by a board specially constituted for that purpose, and not by a court. Now, one reason for that was this:	we found in that province for
many years that men having claims and finally succeeding against their employer would discover that the lawyer cabbaged all the damages and these poor fellows got nothing. One object in introducing the Compensation Act in Ontario was that the man or his widow, or his fatherless children, would get whatever they were entitled to without any cost. I am not familiar with the Compensation Act of the province of New Brunswick, but I fancy that it is in some respects at least like the one that exists in Ontario. There is not much left to a board-
'Mr. COFP: It is left to the judge of the court there.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: It is determined by the statute that a man shall be entitled to a certain percentage of the wages that he earned for the twelve months previous to his injury or death.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: That depends on the degree of the injury.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
-and is fixed by the statute. So that, if the law in New Brunswick or in any other province is like the law in Ontario, there is very little left to the board, and it is not worth while arguing that one board would award larger sums for damages than another. They are restricted by the terms of the statute to pay a certain percentage of the wages earned during the preceding year. That, however, is the case in Ontario. I rose, Mr. Chairman, to set my hon. friend from Kamour-aska (Mr. E. Lapointe) right. If I understood him correctly, he was attacking one of the reports of my department. I think he misread the clause altogether. He read the following:
In 1916 laws in the field of labour legislation wore passed by the Federal Government and by the legislatures of all the provinces except Prince Edward Island.
I gathered from what he said that he understood that laws affecting wages or compensation were passed. Well, he says he did not mean that, so there is no discrepancy. There were laws passed in 1916 affecting labour, but he spoke about the modern legislation. The article contained these words:
The enactment of modern compensation laws *by four provinces brings Canada fairly well in line with the rapid development of legi*tion of this kind throughout the world.
His statement was that we had said that there were compensation Acts passed in four of the provinces, and that some one else had said that such laws were in effect in either seven or nine provinces. What we refer to here is modern compensation laws. There never was a time, I think, in any part of the British Empire, when a servant had not the right to bring an action against his employer for damages resulting from the negligence of his employer. But several abuses grew up in England, as well as in some parts of Canada, where what is known as contributory negligence was brought in, where fellow-servants were brought in, where it was held that if a man were injured while in the employ of another man through the negligence of a fellow-servant he could not recover anything from his employer, because when he hired to his employer he took his chances of any negligence that a fellow-servant might be guilty of. I do not think that principle was ever adopted in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
It was a very erroneous principle, but it grew up in Ontario to such an extent that they have held there that a sectionman working on a railroad was a fellow-employee with the superintendent of the road living in Chicago, and if he were injured by reason of the negligence of the superintendent in Chicago he could not recover anything because of that fellow-servant principle. This Compensation Act has done away with contributory negligence altogether, and with that principle or doctrine of co-service, a fellow-service, fellow-workmen or fellow-servant. But. as I said a moment ago, there never was a time when under the common law of England a servant could not recover from his employer for negligence by the employer himself. Well, it was thought a hardship that he could not recover where the negli-

gence was on the part of his superior officer, or the manager, or the superintendent of the road, and a Compensation Act was passed many years ago in Ontario-not what is referred to in the article quoted from as a modern Compensation Act, but one passed more than twenty years ago making an employer liable in certain cases to his servant for the negligence of a superior officer. But the modern Act, passed in 1914, does away entirely with the question of contributory negligence and the doctrine of co-service or fellow-service, allowing a man a certain percentage of the wages that he earned during the twelve months next preceding the time when he was injured. If he is killed his widow gets a certain amount of money per month while she remains a widow, and each child receives a certain amount per month until it reaches a certain age. So that these boards in Ontario have very little latitude after all.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Might I ask the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) to determine in the Bill what procedure will be followed in an action against the Crown? Will it be the provincial procedure, ot the procedure followed in the Exchequer Court?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
It would not be the same as in the Exchequer Court, because he would not be suing in the Exchequer Court. He would be suing in the court that had jurisdiction in the province. The only question that comes up then is the question of service, and the ordinary law would apply as to what would be service for the Crown. In actions against the Crown with respect to railway claims under $500, special provision is made for service on railway agents on the line. This procedure would not apply in this case. I have not looked into the point to see just what would he service on the Crown, but that would be for the judge in the case to determine. I do not think it is necessary here to go to the extent of fixing what is service on the Crown, nor do I think it would be wise to legislate that service on officers of the Crown situated in far-off provinces, would be service, for the reason that this Act is so very wide, enabling suits to be lodged against the Crown by employees of any department whatever. I do not think it would be wise to facilitate service in' such a way as to enable a man to serve some one at a great distance- perhaps a comparatively minor employee- and obtain judgment before there could be even notice upon those who were responsible to refute or dispute the claim. I think we had better leave it to the application of the ordinary law for the time

being, and not provide means for facilitat- " ing service.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Will service be on the Attorney General?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Leave it to the application of the law. I would not undertake to advise what the law would be.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
The matter of service is
a very important one. In this case the proceedings would be against the Minister of Railways-

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
It might be against
any department.

COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Why not appoint a committee of business men-not lawyers-*' to fix it up?

speechtext:
Suppose we appoint ex-
Ministers of Militia and Defence.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
No more dangerous suggestion could be adopted than that of my hon. friend (Mr. Jacobs). Nothing is more dangerous than for one legislative body to interfere with the machinery of another.
If there is any trouble in the province of Quebec, let the persons interested go to the Quebec legislature and get it remedied.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: May I ask-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I must remind the hon. member that the rale which says that the rules of the House must be observed in committee with the exception that a member may speak more than once should not be interpreted to mean that more than one member may speak at the same time.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: My hon. friend simply wanted to speak more thani once.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) is quite correct in asking that

this clause be put through as it was drawn. He says that the parliamentary counsel, the solicitor of his department, and the Chairman of the Board of Rail-10 p.m. way Commissioners assisted in drafting the clause, and it is not likely that by getting up one after the other in a haphazard way we can reasonably declare the law better than that tribunal of three. I think that some members who have spoken have not realized the difference between a court and a board.
A court determines whether there is liability on the part of the employer; a board assumes that there is liability. In Ontario there is no question of whether there is liability or not; every employee has a remedy.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Certainly, it is the same all over.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The whole point is as to the amount of the compensation. The Government think that they should have a right to determine the compensation from time to time, and if in their opinion the boards are not proceeding on a proper basis, the Dominion, as the-superior legislative body, should have the right to take action in the matter. That would not affect any railway employee, as some hon. gentlemen have contended, because his claim would be decided before any change was made.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
In our province the
court decides not that there is liability, but the amount of the damages. Liability is created by law, and the amount of compensation is limited. But what we want to know is how we are going to serve, and where. If I sue the Minister of Public Works, where am I to serve him? If I sue the Department of Customs, where am I to serve the Department of Customs? In such cases II am suing His Majesty the King; where am I to notify him that he is to appear? If we are to have an Act to help employees of the Government, let us give them the means of bringing the King before the proper tribunal in order that he may answer the demands made upon him for compensation.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I am surprised to hear
the member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat), who represents such a large railway constituency, say that he is satisfied with the general provisions of this Act so far as compensation is concerned. The particulars of the Bill are practically the same as the terms of the resolution. I am not satisfied with the provisions of the Bill respecting compensation. 1 was glad to
hear the Minister of Railways say that this is a measure of temporary relief, and that the Government propose to bring in a measure of compensation which will apply to the whole of Canada. The first objection I have to the general principle of this Bill is that the compensation which will be awarded to the same class of employees throughout the Dominion is not uniform. A man may be injured on a railway in Ontario and when he seeks compensation he is brought under the terms of the Compensation Act in force in that province. He then appears before a board, and that board determine whether or not they have jurisdiction over the action which has brought aJbout the injury. Their decision is final and no further compensation or damage can be recovered against the employer, or, consequently, against the Dominion Government. In Saskatchewan they have not a modern Compejneation Act, but an Act which places the administration of such cases in the hands of the district court. The man who receives an injury, even if he was slightly negligent, would be entitled to recover damages. The measure of the damage for accident to which he would Ibe entitled is determined by the various clauses of the statute, and, in the case of death, the amount which his dependents could recover is limited, I think, to $1,800. In Ontario the limit is $2,500. We must note this distinction: Under the Compensation Act of Ontario, once the board assumes jurisdiction to determine . the amount of damage, the amount which they assess is limited to $2,500 and there is no possible recovery beyond that. Under the Saskatchewan Act-the same Act is in force in Alberta-where a man is injured or where a man has been killed and leaves dependents the injured man or the dependents have the right to elect whether they shall proceed for the recovery of damages under the Chmpensation .Act or in an action at common law.
That is a matter of great importance to the dependent family. A man may be killed by the negligence of a railway corporation, and an action may be brought under the Compensation Act. In Ontario, $2,500 is the limit that can be awarded under the Compensation Act, but if an action were brought at common law in Saskatchewan or in the other provinces which have similar Acts, for that act of negligence, the railway corporation or the employer, whoever he or it might be, would be assessed in damages which would be adequate compensation; it might be $5,000, $8,000, $10,000 or $15,000 the dependents would receive. I believe

that when we adopt the compensation Acts of the provinces we are taking away from the employees the right which they may have at common law, that is, assuming that this Government intends to give to employees the right to bring an action against the Crown. I think that whatever scheme of compensation is adopted by this Parliament for the benefit of Government employees in this country should establish, first, that they may have tiheir remedy under the Compensation Act, if they so desire and wish to recover damages for something in the nature of an accident, or secondly, that they may bring an action at common law. I think the Minister of Railways, when he discusses this matter fully with the representative of the railway organizations, will find that that is the principle which they have in mind, because I have discussed this matter with a great many railway men in the West and know their viewpoint. While they appreciate, no doubt, what the Government is doing for them, I trust that when the minister has had an opportunity of looking into this he will introduce a compensation Act into this Parliament which shall apply to all employees of this Government throughout the whole Dominion.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Will this Act apply to employees of the Canadian Northern railway?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The Canadian Northern railway comes under the provincial Acts, just the same as the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk.

Subsection agreed to.
On section 1, subsection 4-employees on Government railways must elect between Railway Provident Societies benefits and this Act:
Mr. W1GMORE: Does this mean that members of the Provident Fund will not share in this compensation?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
When this Bill was being drafted, I -sent for representatives of the Provident Fund and discussed the matter with them; and we have had the Bill drafted so as not to interfere with their rights in lany way. The Provident Fund Act was passed in 1907, and to that fund the Dominion Government subscribes $100,000 per annum. Members of tbe fund have a great many different rights; they are pensioned for life, for instance, and receive so many weeks' pay in case of injury, and so on. The Object of this clause is not to take away any rights a member of the Provident Fund would have under the

fund in the case of injuries or death by aocident. There is a beard of . managers of the Provident Fund, and they have regulations governing the amount that shall be paid (for different injuries, and I think there is also- an amount payable in case of death. The Compensation Acts of the different provinces provide compensation only for injuries or death, whereas the Provident Fund has a long list of benefits. One of the representatives of the Intercolonial railway was here with the 'solicitor of the Railway Department for two or three days, and it was agreed to put this clause in and see how it would work out between now and next session. If it does not work out as we expect, then we can provide any remedy that is thought desirable next session. I do not wish to interfere with the members of the Provident Fund in iamy way. I want the railway employees to have all the benefits that are coming to them under the Provident Fund, but in case of death their dependents can go under the Provident Fund ot under this Act, whichever they desire, but not both; that is the only object of this clause.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I am surprised at the Minister of Railways. He was posing a moment ago' las >a philanthropist who wanted to see the railway employees get as much as they could. Now we see him in a different light entirely. The Minister of Railways ought to know, or the law officers of the Crown ought to know, that a member of the Provident Fund pays into the fund a certain sum of money as insurance, and when this insurance becomes a claim, he is entitled to a certain sum of money, irrespective of any other sums he may receive from the Government. He pays for this insurance, and the Government has no Tight to ask him to elect whether he will accept one or the other. The Provident Funds of Railway Company employees and their rights thereunder have received judicial interpretation by the Privy Council in the case of Miller versus the Grand Trunk railway, and I am sure that if the law officers of the Crown had studied that case they would not have advised the Minister of Railways to bring before Parliament a clause of this kind, which is subversive of all the rules of law laid down [DOT]by the highest court in the realm.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
The reason I asked my question was because I had the same point in my mind as my hon. friend. I do not think it is fair or just to discriminate against a member of the Provident Fund. While the Government are paying $100,000

into this fund, the members of the fund are also paying in a -certain sum every month, or every year, and I do not think they should be discriminated against. They pay this amount every month just as a man may pay the premium on his insurance policy.
I understand-the minister will correct me if I am wrong-that the majority of the employees of the Intercolonial railway are members of the Provident Fund, and some of them have been paying into it for years.
I think this is a clear case of discrimination.
I think -they should be allowed to draw whatever benefit they have a right to derive from the provident fund, and should share -also in any benefit they are entitled to share in under the Workmen's Compensation Act. I think it is clearly a case of discrimination against 'the men in the provident fund. The hon. minister says he has considered this very carefully with the employees of the Intercolonial and that they are satisfied with this. I am very much surprised to hear that they were satisfied.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Before preparing this Bill, or deciding on it, I had the solicitor send for a representative of the Provident Fund of the Intercolonial railway.
Mr. E. fLAPOINTE:	Not of the employees?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Of course it was an
employee of the Intercolonial who was a member of the Provident Fund Board. We discussed it at times during two or three days, and I understand they agreed to this clause, and were satisfied with it. The way we discussed it was thie: we are paying $100,000 into this fund

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
You pay that much each
year?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Yes-and the idea was that if an employee were injured and received, -as compensation for the injury, a certain amount from the Provident Fund, to which fund we were paying $100,000 per annum, and also received money under the Compensation Act, he would be twice paid for his injury. There was no intention

and I have no desire-to discriminate* against the employees in the Provident Fund. We talked this over, -and thought this clause was fair. This Bill may have been prepared hurriedly. I will have to take this Bill up. again, probably in the recess, and see how it works, and if there is any discrimination or anything unfair in any way, shape or form, so far as the employees are concerned, I will remedy it at the next session of Parliament.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Some years ago, I think in 1906 or 1907, a tentative Bill was presented in this Parliament by the railway companies. They wanted to avoid their liability when one of their employees had been killed or injured, if the family was receiving money from the insurance fund which was provided by the company. At the request of Parliament, the question *was submitted to the Supreme Court, with an appeal to the Privy Council. I remember Mr. Justice Lennox, then member of the House, represented the railway employees. The matter came up before the Privy Council, and they decided to the best of my recollection, that the railway company-I think it was Miller vs. Grand Trunk-were liable, even where the family of an employee had received money from the insurance fund. It seems to me this case is absolutely similar.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I have no other object in view than the one I stated. I have been trying to make the Bill fit in with the law of the provinces in regard to other railways. If there is nothing in the way, other than the difficulty which has been suggested, I would remedy that at the very first opportunity, at the next session, and, therefore, having gone into the matter with the little time I had at my disposal with the official of the railways-

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: And the employees?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Yes; I cannot remember the names of the employees representing the Provident Fund, but it was a railway employee-I am not going to take any advantage in any way, but would like to have the Bill passed in its present shape, and see how it works from now until next session.
Mr. WIGMiORE: The Canadian Pacific railway have an organization the same as the Intercolonial, a provident fund you might call it, and yet, when it comes to a question of their rights under the Compensation Act of the different provinces, they receive the benefit under those Acts, just the same as if they were not receiving a benefit from the Provident Fund. It ie exactly the same as the Provident Fund of the Intercolonial. Therefore, I claim this is a pure discrimination against the men in the Provident Fund.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
If the hon. minister wants to put the Government employees in ^ the same position as other employees, why this clause? My hon. friend spoke of the case of Miller versus Grand Trunk railway. The same principle has been affirmed

several times in cases against the Intercolonial railway or the King. In my own practice I have had a few cases of this kind, and the Intercolonial railway has always tried to plead this clause in the Provident Fund to get rid of the liability, but the Exchequer Court has always decided that the employee was entitled to the damages, as well as to the amount due from the Provident Fund. This Provident Fund is a sort of natural insurance. The employee is paying for that, and it is not optional either. The very day a man enters the service of the Intercolonial Tailway he becomes a member of that insurance fund. He must be a member'of the insurance fund, and every month a certain amount is kept out of his salary by the treasurer of the railway. Why should there be a discrimination of this kind against the employees of the Intercolonial railway, when the employees of other railways are entitled to both the compensation and insurance, which they must receive when their death is caused by an accident? The hon. minister is not improving the position of the employee by this clause. He is taking away something to which they were entitled before this legislation.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: In comparison^ with the $100,000 paid by the Government into this fund, what do the men's contributions amount to?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I could not tell you this evening.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: The hon. minister has stated to the House that the employees or their representative had been conferred with, and had agreed to this section. If that is so, I will not have very much more to say in regard to it, but I Teally think that they must have misunderstood the situation or they would not have agreed to such an unreasonable proposition being placed upon the statute book, which would take away from them the very equitable right that they should have in a case of this kind. I am glad to hear the hon. minister say that he will remedy the matter, if any difficulty occurs. I have not had any communication from the railway men whatever, and if I were Minister of Railways T would be very sorry to take the responsibility of taking away from the railway employees the rights they have had for so many years under this Act.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
Instead of taking away any rights, I believe it gives them more rights than they had before. Some gentleman, a stranger, was introduced to me, and 
said he was a representative of the Rai'way Provident Fund. We discussed the matter two or three times. He was an employee of the Intercolonial railway, as I understood. I am only stating the matter as I gathered it from this gentleman. We agreed on this proposition in the meantime. We agreed on this in the meantime and if it is not fair or right we can remedy it next session.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: In the face of the decision of the Privy Council, does the hon. gentleman persist in forcing this Bill through the House?

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: I persist in doing what I believe is fair and right .and what has been agreed upon by the employees of the railway.

maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.

In the next place, even if there had been, this Bill does not take away any right without substituting another and a fair right. I do not think my hon. friend, as a lawyer acting for his client, would have any great cause for complaint if we took away the very shadowy, nebulous right which his office thinks it has in this case and provided him with the substantial and very certain right which he would have here.
Mr. iMdMASTER: The nebulous right is a right in satisfaction of which one department has offered $2,000, but we consider it is sufficiently devoid of nebulousness to warrant us in pressing for $5,000.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext: Many a thousand dollars has been paid by the departments in respect to losses as an act of grace on the part of the Crown and not as a matter of right. It is the same in this case. maintopic: COMPENSATION FOR INJURIES TO GOVERNMENT EMPLOYEES.
speechtext:
I believe that this legislation is good, but I would not like the minister to imagine that previous to the adoption of this measure a workman on the Intercolonial had no recourse against the Crown. We have been suing the Crown time and again as a result of accidents. Recourse was more difficult than it will be now. We had to prove statutory negligence. When there was no statutory negligence proved the action was dismissed. We have obtained compensation for employees of the railway in many instances and it was not all a matter of grace on the part of the Crown, as the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) suggested. These cases have been carried to the Supreme Court and the Privy Council. Section 20 of the Exchequer Court Act states:
The Exchequer Court shall have exclusive jurisdiction to hear and determine all claims against the Crown arising out of any death or injury to the person or property and every claim against the Crown arising under any law of Canada.
I think it would be well to insert in subsection (1) of this Bill the words " notwithstanding anything in the Exchequer Cburt Act."

speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. J. D. Reid (Minister of Railways and Canals), Bill No. 52, to amend the Department of Railways and Canals Act, was read the second time and the House went into committee on the Bill, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section 20-Stores Accounts, Limitation®.
Mr.. J. D. REID: The object of the Bill is simply to increase the amount of stores which the Canadian Government railways may keep on hand at one time from $1,500,000 to $6,000,000. The reason for the change is this:	When the Railways and Canals
Act was passed a number of years ago, the Government only owned the Intercolonial railway. Since then the Transcontinental, the Intercolonial and other railways have been .added to the Government system. Requirement® have increased to such an extent that we could not possibly operate these railways, without increasing the amount of .stores that we may have on hand. For some time we really have been operating almost in violation of the law in the extent of the stores that we have been carrying, and the Auditor General insisted that we should have a vote sufficient to cover all requirements. On the eastern lines at the present time Stores Account is as. follows:	Fuel, $1,110,000; ties, $200,-
000; General, $1,706,400; making a total of $3,016,400. In the case of the western lines the Stores Account stands as follows: Fuel, $1,176,000; ties, $10,700; General, $1,026,000, a total of $2,212,700 and a grand total of $5,229,100. We are getting in large stores of coal for the coming yeaT, and for that reason we are asking Parliament to increase the amount to be voted for that purpose.
Section agreed to, Bill reported and read the third time.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext: The Minister of Trade and Commerce this afternoon explained the object of his Bill. The hon. member knows that the Customs Department, for instance, issue a blue-book every year of customs statistics, and the Trade and Commerce Department issue another, and other departments issue their own statistics. The object of the bureau is to compile them altogether. Each department, of course, must gather its own statistics and hand them over to the Trade andi Commerce Department, and there they will all be compiled in one volume. In that way, you have them all together under one department to be put before the public in book form. That was the object of the Bill. The hon. member will quite understand that, in each of the departments where it is necessary to compile statistics, you must have employees to gather these statistics.

Some men have said to me, comparing the statistics of trade issued by the Customs Department with those issued by the Trade and Commerce Department: They are not the same; you should get the different departments together, see that they are right, and then publish statistics that are accurate. Fair Wages and Inspection Officers, $15,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY.
speechtext:
What is the special purpose of this appropriation?
Mr. iCROTHERS: We have, I think, five fair wage officers. They are called fair wage officers, because when they were originally appointed their work was largely

confined to fixing schedules of wages on public works. We are not doing very much by way of public works now and have not been for some years, neither has their work been confined to that sort of thing. They are largely employed in settling disputes and differences between employers and employees before these reach the stage where a board of conciliation is applied for. For instance, we have >a man located at Vancouver. Some six years ago we had only two of these men, both located at Ottawa. These differences between employers and employees often arise in a few hours, and previously, if they occurred at Vancouver or Sydney, a big strike might be on before our men could get to these distant places. One of the first things I did was to send to Vancouver one of the best men we had, so that he would be right on the ground to hear the rumblings of labour disturbances and to check them before they became serious. This man has saved the Government many thousands of dollars; he has kept men at work who would otherwise have been on strike and, on the whole, has rendered very valuable service by being on the ground. We appointed other men at Calgary, Winnipeg and Saskatoon, and they did valuable work in assisting in the maintenance of industrial peace. We have been especially fortunate in keeping our working people at work; no serious disturbances have occurred in Canada since the outbreak of war. That speaks well for the employers and employees, as well as for those officers who have devoted their best efforts to keeping things running smoothly. These are the men mentioned here as fair wage officers.
